news.title: AI anxiety is sweeping the globe — and cutting across party lines: poll
news.text: The freakout over AI that started in Silicon Valley and led to growing American calls to pause development has swept Western countries. A new POLITICO Poll finds that pluralities of adults in the US, Canada, and Europe want to pause AI development regardless of their political leanings — and most believe there's a real risk the technology could destroy humanity. Pluralities of respondents in several countries say it's okay for their country to fall behind others in the development of AI if it means being more responsible and secure when advancing it. And they're more likely to expect AI will destroy jobs rather than create them. The results from the poll, conducted by independent polling firm Public First, illustrate the sheer magnitude of how AI fears are spreading as some industry leaders warn the technology's advancement could have potentially grave consequences. They show people's preference for caution, even at the risk of forfeiting what could be revolutionary advancements or their country falling behind in the broader AI race. And for governments, the results offer a stark warning of the political backlash they may face if they don't take steps to rein in the technology, as leaders from US President Donald Trump to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham scramble their responses. Across six countries — the US, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Spain, and Germany — roughly half of adults surveyed said AI is good enough now, so they supported a pause on further development to reduce risks, rather than continuing development for added benefits. That sentiment was highest in the UK at 51% and lowest in Germany at 45%. Meanwhile, just 30% to 40% of adults in each country favored continued development to bring about "significant benefits." An even greater share of adults — more than half in every country surveyed and up to almost two-thirds in the US, France, the UK, and Canada — said there was at least a "moderate" risk that the technology could "destroy humanity." The skepticism around AI could impact Europe's ability to keep up in the global competition: The European Union, which has taken a cautionary approach by adopting the world's first AI regulation in 2024, hosts almost no providers of frontier AI models, with French Mistral as the most worthy contender. The bloc's highest official, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, leaned into the calls for a pause, saying during her yearly address last week that "if the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too." She's invited the main AI labs to talk about how the EU could "support" industry efforts to pace the frontier. But the recent AI warnings have put European policymakers in a tough spot, as the EU spent most of last year focusing on catching up in the race by preparing to invest billions in compute capacity and trying to boost low AI adoption rates. European policymakers faced additional pressure from activists on Monday, when the Pause AI movement demonstrated in front of the European Parliament buildings in Brussels. "We would not board a plane with a one-in-ten-chance of exploding mid-air," said Didier Coeurnelle, the coordinator of PauseAI Belgium, referring to the recent assessment from an Anthropic employee that there's a higher than 10% chance AI could wipe out humanity. "That is what we are tolerating with AI today." Calls for slowing AI development have gone mainstream after AI titans including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk raised the idea in recent days. Consensus on the issue quickly fell apart in America after Trump blasted the AI warnings as a "HOAX," sinking the likelihood of an immediate bipartisan deal to regulate AI. Since then, other industry leaders including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House adviser David Sacks have similarly downplayed the technology's dangers and resisted calls for new government regulations, blaming alarmists for overinflating AI risks. "This poll fits the classic techno-panic pattern: few harms today, plenty of fear about tomorrow," said Neil Chilson, head of AI policy at the U.S.-based Abundance Institute. Chilson pointed to the POLITICO Poll finding that in every country but Spain, a third of respondents — or more — had rarely or never used AI. "Most people haven't felt AI's benefits but they've heard many scary stories about its future," he added. "For now, fear is outrunning experience. But experience will catch up." Still, many Republican and Democratic state leaders have scrambled to push for stronger controls, defying Trump's and the federal government's hands-off approach. In California, the global epicenter of the AI industry, politicians are also tightening regulations as voters there sour on the technology. On Friday, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom — a likely 2028 presidential candidate — signed an executive order accelerating the implementation of new AI oversight standards and tasked state agencies with exploring whether a mandatory "kill switch" is needed for the most advanced AI models. As politicians in America and beyond heed the warnings, so too, do voters. According to the poll, people across North America and Europe view industry researchers' warnings as legitimate. When asked whether AI lab staff really believed their own fears that "AI will kill us all" or if they were making a "marketing move" to hype their products, adults from all six countries tended to view the warnings as genuine. That's despite a suggestion among some industry observers that frontier AI companies may have sought to benefit from the publicity around their models. "I think a lot of it is marketing, to overemphasize the proposed capabilities," Max Junestrand, co-founder and CEO of Legora, an American-Swedish AI firm valued at over $5 billion, said in an interview when asked about this summer's AI hacking incidents. Wariness of rapid AI development and its risks to society mostly crossed party lines in Europe and Canada. In the US, it was slightly more partisan: Americans who had voted for Trump in 2024 split almost evenly when asked whether to pause advanced AI development (44%) or press forward (40%), and they were more inclined than those who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 to say that AI employees' alarmist talk was a marketing stunt. Nearly half of Trump voters also said the US shouldn't allow itself to fall behind other countries in the AI development race, even if it means taking risks to stay ahead. In comparison, majorities in Canada and the UK (53%) opted for falling behind on AI advancement to prioritize security, even if it meant potentially ceding a technological edge to other countries. Tyler Katzenberger reported from Sacramento, California, and Pieter Haeck reported from Brussels. This edition of The POLITICO Poll was conducted by Public First from Sept. 13 to 15, surveying more than 2,000 respondents each from the U.S., Canada, U.K., France, Spain and Germany, and has an overall margin of error of ±2.2 percentage points. Smaller subgroups have higher margins of error. This story originally appeared on POLITICO and is courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms.

news.title: Harris keeps 2028 door open as she hits midterm campaign trail, warns ‘28 won’t matter’ without 2026
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris said Tuesday that she has not decided whether she will run for president again in 2028, telling voters in Detroit that the upcoming midterm elections must come first. Harris was directly asked during a fireside chat whether she had thought about running for president in 2028 and whether another White House campaign was "on your plate." "I have not decided if I'm going to run again," Harris said before turning the focus to the midterms. "I do, I do sincerely believe 28 won't matter if we don't get through 26." GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS Harris said she was focused on traveling the country and reminding voters of the power of their voices ahead of the 2026 elections. "And I'm a big believer that you can be. When you focus on the thing out there, you trip on the thing over here." The exchange came during Harris' second event Tuesday in Detroit, where she participated in a fireside chat moderated by Rev. Dr. Wendell Anthony, president of the Detroit Branch NAACP and pastor of Fellowship Chapel, and Rev. Dr. Genetta Y. Hatcher, pastor of The Room Church. Before asking Harris about a possible 2028 campaign, Anthony encouraged those in attendance to vote and referenced early and mail-in voting. Harris was later presented with "take your souls to the polls" merchandise. KAMALA HARRIS CLAIMS GOP 'CHEATING' AHEAD OF MIDTERMS, SAYS SHE'S FOCUSED ON STOPPING THE 'MADNESS' Earlier Tuesday, Harris campaigned alongside Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health and healthcare costs. Harris used the event to criticize President Donald Trump's healthcare policies and voice support for El-Sayed. Harris' remarks came as she focuses on the 2026 midterms while leaving open the possibility of another presidential campaign. Harris became the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 after then-President Joe Biden ended his re-election campaign. news.title: Democratic Governor’s Wealth Surges by 10 Figures
news.text:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has seen his personal fortune grow by more than $1 billion since he took office in 2019, according to a new estimate.

The Hyatt hotel heir has also fueled speculation about a possible presidential campaign after opening up about the significant health changes he has been pursuing.

Forbes estimates that Pritzker is now worth approximately $4.2 billion, placing him among the names featured on the magazine’s 2026 World’s Billionaires list.

His wealth climbed by more than $500 million over the past year alone. Despite that increase, Pritzker fell from 979th to 1,108th among the world’s wealthiest people.

If elected president, he would become the second billionaire in a row to hold the office, following Donald Trump.

Much of Pritzker’s fortune comes from his family’s hotel empire. He also previously led a private equity firm with his brother before leaving the business in 2017.

The Pritzker family ranks among America’s most powerful wealthy dynasties, with 13 family members currently recognized as billionaires.

Our News Outlet has contacted Gov. Pritzker for comment.

Pritzker has disclosed that he began taking a GLP-1 medication two years ago after receiving a diabetes diagnosis.

The 61-year-old Democrat said the treatment has helped him lose 80 pounds. In a Monday interview with CBS, he said he feels “a whole lot different and a whole lot better.”

He said his concerns about the health risks of being overweight were shaped in part by the death of his father, who suffered a fatal heart attack at age 39.

“He was actually quite an active person, even though he was overweight, and so he was on a tennis court and had a heart attack, and my mother was there, and he died in her arms,” Pritzker said.

Pritzker said the demands of public office contributed to further weight gain. His size has also made him a frequent target of mockery from Trump.

“Pritzker, I don’t know, he’s too busy eating,” Trump said at a 2024 campaign rally. “He wants to eat all the time.”

His doctor prescribed the medication after blood tests conducted two years ago showed that Pritzker had diabetes.

“My doctor said, ‘Oh, no, you’ll never come off of it. You’re going to have to do this the rest of your life, and I recommend that you take a GLP-1,’” Pritzker recalled.

He said the effects were noticeable almost immediately, with a two-pound loss during his first week and a marked reduction in his appetite.

“All of a sudden, on the third day, I was like, you know, actually, I don’t need to eat that thing,” Pritzker said.

‘But it was the strangest feeling. Now, I’m not suggesting everything changed in a week. It didn’t happen that way.’

GLP-1s mimic a naturally occurring gut hormone, helping regulate blood sugar and curb appetite by slowing digestion and increasing feelings of fullness. They are used to treat type 2 diabetes and, in some formulations, obesity.

Common brand names include Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide, as well as Mounjaro and Zepbound, which contain tirzepatide, a related dual GIP/GLP-1 drug. 

The governor announced that Illinois is covering GLP-1s on the state insurance plan for 55,000 civil servants and says that the drug will save money by preventing other diseases.

As well as the drug, Pritzker says that he takes a four-mile walk each morning along Lake Michigan to help keep the weight off.

Asked if he was working on his image ahead of a 2028 presidential run, Pritzker replied: ‘I’ve been driven my whole life to lose weight. The fact that I am now able to do it because this GLP-1 became available is truly, like, I mean, it’s something that has meant a lot to me.

‘I have not made any decisions about what I might do in the future. I can tell you I want to be the governor of the state of Illinois for a while longer, and I’m running for reelection.’

The latest Democratic 2028 polling puts Pritzker well behind the early front-runners, despite persistent speculation that the billionaire Illinois governor could mount a White House bid.

A September Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll had Kamala Harris on 17 percent, narrowly ahead of Pete Buttigieg on 16 percent, with Gavin Newsom and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez both on 14 percent. Pritzker was not among the candidates registering support in the poll’s leading tier.

A separate Harvard CAPS/Harris survey earlier this month placed Pritzker at 4 percent, behind Harris on 42 percent, Newsom on 18 percent, Buttigieg and Ocasio-Cortez on 9 percent apiece, and Josh Shapiro and Jon Ossoff on 7 percent.

news.title: Kamala Harris says 'attack on DEI is an attack on maternal care' in appearance with El-Sayed
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday declared that an attack on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) is an attack on maternal care as she joined Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit to rally support ahead of the November midterm elections. Harris made the remarks during a campaign roundtable with El-Sayed and several healthcare advocates focused on Black maternal health and healthcare costs. "An attack on DEI, to recognize diversity, equity and inclusion, is an attack by definition on maternal care, including the need to protect Black women in connection with their pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care," Harris said. She noted that maternal mortality rates are disproportionately higher among minority groups, with the risk of death increasing up to four times for Black women and three times for Native women. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES "One in 12 women in America currently lives in a maternal care desert with limited or no access to maternal care," she added. Harris then took aim at political leaders who tout "family values," arguing that efforts to end DEI programs strip away protections aimed at supporting certain communities during pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care. BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT "As one of the most, some would say the most financially strong economies in the world, we have the distinction of also having one of the highest rates of maternal mortality in the world," she said. "So it raises the issue of disparities and also hypocrisy when there are leaders who otherwise walk around every day talking about their family values." Harris also turned her criticism toward President Donald Trump’s health care legislation, which she referred to as the "Big Bad Bill," arguing that it cut Medicaid spending with the support of former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee facing El-Sayed. DR. OZ UNVEILS MEDICAID OVERHAUL, CLAMPS DOWN ON $2B FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS AND MANDATES WORK FOR ABLE-BODIED "Medicaid is the largest funder for maternity care in America," she said. "Donald Trump cut Medicaid funding by a trillion dollars. These are the facts Mike Rogers supported that cut through that ‘Big Bad Bill.’" Harris closed by reaffirming her support for El-Sayed in the Senate race, pointing to his position on maternal health and saying she believes he would be a "champion" on the issue. news.title: CNN’s polling guru calls the 2028 Democratic field a ‘mess’
news.text:
Democratic voters remain deeply divided over a potential nominee for the 2028 presidential race, according to new polling from Bowling Green State University and YouGov.

The survey placed former Vice President Kamala Harris in a tight race at the top of a crowded pack, with 17 percent support among Democratic voters.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg closely followed at 16 percent, while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and California Governor Gavin Newsom polled at 14 percent each.

Reviewing the data on “CNN News Central,” CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten described the early primary landscape as exceptionally scattered, comparing the party’s primary base to people who “don’t know what the heck they want.”

“There are four folks within 17 percent, I mean, it’s just completely messy,” Enten said. “The clear thing to take away here is there is no clear leader in this group. This is a field that is messier than any Democratic field in at least 20 years. I would argue, the messiest, least clear Democratic field since 1992.”

Enten noted that the current primary environment differs significantly from prior cycles, calling the lineup the party’s “messiest” in decades and joking that “it’s messier than an airport the Sunday after Thanksgiving.”

Addressing Harris’s standing, CNN host Kate Bolduan asked how her current support compared with her earlier popularity among Democrats. Enten highlighted her sharp drop in numbers since the summer of 2024.

“You see the 17 percent now, back in July of 2024, just as Joe Biden was getting out of the race, Kamala Harris was polling at 45 percent,” Enten said. “You know, that’s more than twice as much as the support that she has right now.”

Enten compared her position with President Donald Trump’s early lead ahead of the 2024 Republican primary, when Trump held 49 percent support among GOP voters.

“This is a weak place for a frontrunner,” Enten said. “These are the types of numbers that would really make me think twice about running if I was Kamala Harris, given her universal name recognition.”

The polling metrics were released hours before Harris was scheduled to join Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a campaign stop in Michigan. 

The trip to the battleground state reignited questions about her potential 2028 plans, though Harris has not publicly announced or committed to another campaign.
news.summary: Four potential candidates remain within three percentage points of each other at the top of new 2028 polling, led narrowly by former Vice President Kamala Harris
news.author: Jasmine Fernández

news.title: Kamala Harris Calls Trump’s Media Ban ‘Absolutely Abhorrent’
news.text:
Kamala Harris called President Donald Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House “absolutely abhorrent.”

On Tuesday, the former vice president was stopped while getting in a car by CBS News, among other outlets, and was asked what her thoughts were on the media ban. She replied while getting into her car.

“The man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing,” Harris told CBS News’ Aaron Navarro. “He’s trying to stifle the ability of journalists to let the people of America know what’s really going on with their government.”

Watch her response below.

Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House grounds Friday. Reporters from the outlets were denied access to the White House on Saturday and CNN was removed from its duties as the White House pool representative for television networks on Monday. 

This backfired on the president Monday when CNN was slated to represent as the pool videographers for one of his events, but it could not be heard because the camera operators and sound people were not allowed on site. 

The five major television networks — Fox News Media, ABC News, CBS News, CNN and NBC News — that make up the White House TV pool suspended pooled television coverage of President Trump on Monday after the White House prevented CNN from fulfilling its scheduled duties.

The banned outlets noted that their access was removed “without notice or process” and that the move from the president threatens press freedom and “the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” 

CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit against the president, arguing that he imposed the ban over what he sees as negative-only news media coverage. The case was assigned to a federal judge, who was nominated by Trump and previously sided with CNN when the White House attempted to expel one of its White House reporters in 2018. The organizations are seeking a temporary restraining order restoring their access.

The White House Correspondents’ Association also called on the Trump administration to restore the outlets’ access, saying the government should not determine which journalists can cover the president based on whether officials approve of their reporting.

news.title: Kamala Harris backs El-Sayed, says Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat is key
news.text:
Stressing the national importance of Michigan's role in the 2026 midterms, former Vice President and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris stopped in Detroit and threw her support behind Abdul El-Sayed, Democrats' pick for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat.

She endorsed him at Birth Detroit, a community birth center in the city, at the conclusion of a roundtable with the nominee and reproductive health advocates. She said El-Sayed's race against Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake Township will impact affordable health care, childcare and housing.

"That's why I'm here, because these are the big issues that I know impact people across our country, including here in Michigan," she told reporters.

During the event, she recalled serving alongside now-retiring Michigan U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, D-Bloomfield Township, saying it gave her a sense of the weight of representing the battleground state.

"His will be a voice — Abdul's — that is a voice representing the people of this state, and it will be a national voice," she said, according to a Fox 2 livestream of the discussion.

During the discussion with Harris on Black maternal health disparities, El-Sayed, who previously served as the health director for Detroit and Wayne County, said his race is about one question — inspired by the venue: "What would we build if we treated all of our kids like all of our kids?" he said.

Ahead of the roundtable, Rogers had characterized Harris' visit as a sign that his Democratic rival's campaign is flailing.

"Desperate times call for desperate measures, and Abdul is so desperate that he’s parachuting Kamala Harris into Michigan to save his flailing campaign," Rogers said in statement.

El-Sayed brushed off the attack when a reporter asked him about it before his meeting with Harris and the others.

"You know what a desperate measure is? Pretending like you didn't back a war that you've been backing for seven months now, calling it a 'win-win-win' then looking at your poll numbers and being like, 'Maybe that was a bad idea,'" he said, referring to Rogers' recent call for the war in Iran to "end quickly."

More: Rabbis ask Kamala Harris to talk to Abdul El-Sayed about their concerns

More: Michigan AG Dana Nessel says she will vote for El-Sayed for Senate

Besides highlighting the national importance of Michigan's open Senate race, Harris' appearance could help El-Sayed boost support among Black voters — a traditionally reliable Democratic voting bloc — who backed his primary opponent in the primary.

In Detroit, Michigan's largest majority-Black city, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham secured 62% of the vote to El-Sayed's 34% in August.

Rogers' campaign had a truck outside the roundtable event trying to paint El-Sayed as racist, even as he campaigned inside with the first woman of color to become a major political party's presidential nominee, and a group discussing Black women's health issues.

El-Sayed's primary served as a kind of litmus test for the brand of progressive politics he espouses, including his calls for Medicare for All and ending unconditional military aid to Israel.

Now, all eyes are on his race against Rogers, who has the endorsement of President Donald Trump, to see if El-Sayed’s platform carries broad appeal.

"I think this country will vote for an obese, Jewish, Black, homosexual before a woman," Behar said. Guest host Star Jones agreed and added, "We just had one of the most beautiful, brilliant women run for president. And you see what we got." "You don't win on identity alone, and you don't lose on identity alone," co-host Sara Haines pushed back. Alyssa Farah Griffin, the lone Republican co-host, predicted there would be a woman president in the next 20 years. Patrice Onwuka, vice president for economic policy and director of Independent Women's Center for Economic Opportunity, told Fox News Digital, "This warped view is directly the result of elevating identity politics above common sense and connection." KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN "Joy Behar and Star Jones can’t bring themselves to admit that the female candidates they fawned over could not win over the voters," she continued, referencing the four Americans killed in the 2012 Benghazi attacks during Clinton's time as secretary of state and her infamous comment calling Trump supporters "deplorables." "Kamala Harris was a failed vice president who oversaw a massive influx of tens of millions of people into America illegally and ran on vibes rather than making Americans’ lives better," Onwuka added. Sexism may have played a role for some voters, but you can’t take millions of votes and diagnose all of them as sexism." Tell me one woman." During another episode of the show that month, Behar rejected Harris as a potential 2028 candidate. "I love her, she was great, but she didn't win one time. What makes you think she's going to win again?" Behar asked, adding that anyone who thought Harris should run again and could win was not living in reality. During an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said she was weighing a presidential run in 2028, adding, "Pretty candidly, I think about my identity." "I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina," she said. "And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities." news.title: US ex-VP Harris campaigns for leftist El-Sayed in key Senate race
news.text:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (left) and former US vice president Kamala Harris take part in a reproductive health roundtable discussion in Detroit. (AFP pic)
MICHIGAN: Former US vice president Kamala Harris returned to the campaign trail Tuesday alongside a leftist Michigan Senate candidate, seeking to help Democrats hold a crucial battleground seat as speculation persists over another White House run in 2028.
Harris appeared with Abdul El-Sayed at a Detroit-area roundtable on Black maternal health and was scheduled to join other events aimed at mobilising voters in a state central to Democratic hopes of winning control of the Senate in November.
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, faces Republican former congressman Mike Rogers for the seat being vacated by a retiring Democrat.
A Republican victory would make an already challenging Democratic path to a Senate majority considerably steeper.
"The Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration, and I would suggest to you that the fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected," Harris said at the roundtable as she introduced the candidate to the cameras.
The epidemiologist has run in part on his experience in health administration, and he described maternal care as "personal" for him, revealing that two of his father's siblings died before turning five.
"Babies shouldn't die, full stop. And a measure of a society is... the choices we make about the services we provide, about the resources we offer, about the voices we listen to, about the perspective we share or don't share," said El-Sayed.
"Those are the markers of a society, and we have an opportunity in this race to decide that we are going to invest in health care."
The visit put Harris back in the spotlight in Michigan, where Donald Trump narrowly defeated her in the 2024 presidential election and which is set to vote early in the Democratic presidential nominating calendar in 2028.
Harris has said she is "thinking about" another presidential bid but has given no timeline for a decision.
Her Michigan appearance kicks off a broader burst of midterm campaigning, with stops also planned in Nevada and Georgia.
Tuesday's joint appearance was significant for El-Sayed as he seeks to unite Democrats after defeating establishment-backed Representative Haley Stevens in a bruising primary.
El-Sayed drew strong support from the left but performed less strongly among Black voters, a key Democratic constituency in Detroit that Harris's visit could help him reach.
The two Democrats have also occupied different ground over Israel.
El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel and US arms sales to the country, initially backed the "Uncommitted" protest movement against then-president Joe Biden during the 2024 Democratic primary.
Harris, as Biden's vice president, faced anger from Arab and Muslim voters in Michigan over the administration's support for Israel during the Gaza war.
She was also due Tuesday to meet Detroit faith leaders and attend a voter-turnout event involving the local branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People.
news.summary: Kamala Harris returns to the campaign trail to help Democrats hold a crucial Michigan seat as speculation persists over a 2028 White House run.

news.title: The Democrats Have a 2028 Problem
news.text:
Republicans have the luxury of a deep bench. Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and a roster of successful GOP governors give the party real options and a clear direction. Democrats have a crowded stage, and nobody is standing in the spotlight.

The closest thing the Democrats have for a frontrunner is Kamala Harris, and her frontrunner status is superficial at best.

On Tuesday, CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten walked through new 2028 polling, and when anchor Kate Bolduan asked him where Kamala Harris stands, Enten started with the voters themselves.

"[The Democratic base] don't know what the heck they want," Enten said. "This field is historically messy. It's messier than an airport Sunday after Thanksgiving."

The data backs him up. Kamala may lead the pack, but she leads it with a meager 17%. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg sits right behind her at 16%, while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) each pull 14%. That puts four candidates within three points of one another.

"The clear thing to take away here is there is no clear leader in this group," Enten added. "This is a field that is messier than any Democratic field in at least 20 years, I would argue, the messiest, least clear Democratic field since 1992."

ICYMI: The Somali Daycare Fraud Story Just Got Way Bigger Than Minnesota

The bigger story is Kamala's weak performance. In July 2024, just as Joe Biden bowed out of the race, she polled at 45% as Democrats' top choice for the nomination. Today she's at 17%, which means she has shed well over half of her support. Think about that for a second. This is the woman with universal name recognition, the former vice president and a woman of color no less, and the best head start of anyone in the party, and her numbers keep going down. She may be ahead, but her lead is not secure.

Enten offered a useful comparison. "What you really want to be is more where Trump was at this point. Back in the 2024 cycle, he was at 49%," he said. "49% is not anything like 17%. This is a weak place for a frontrunner."

Then he delivered the kicker. "These are the types of numbers that would really make me think twice about running," Enten said.

I still say she is going to run. And her best option is to declare early. But she’s clearly doing some 2028 positioning. The poll dropped just hours before Kamala headed to Michigan to appear alongside Socialist Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for some roundtable event. Appearing with El-Sayed, especially when many establishment Democrats are keeping their distance, is a clear 2028 flex, even though she hasn't announced a campaign or publicly committed to running again.

No clear leader in Democrat 2028 field."This is a field that is messier than any Democratic field in at least 20 years. I would argue, the messiest, least clear democratic field since 1992.” —Harry Enten pic.twitter.com/9YNMrjVfrp— Matt Margolis (@mattmargolis) September 22, 2026

This is a structural problem for the left, and a bad news cycle won't explain it away. The party's pseudo frontrunner is basically neck and neck with several other candidates. Republicans will head into 2028 choosing between strong options. Democrats have had a long time to figure out who they want to lead their party into the future and they still don’t know. So, they will head into 2028 still trying to figure out what they want, and right now, even their own voters can't tell them.
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: Dem Star Drops Bombshell on 2028 Ambitions
news.text:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is openly weighing a 2028 run for either the White House or Senate.

The progressive congresswoman, 36, told The New York Times that she is doing mental “math” as she considers whether to launch a bid for either office.

Ocasio-Cortez has repeatedly been floated as a potential challenger to longtime New York Senator Chuck Schumer, whose seat is up for reelection in 2028, and has been the center of speculation regarding a possible presidential run. 

However, polls show that Ocasio-Cortez faces low favorability ratings that could hinder a future White House bid. In a July CNN/SSRS survey, the New York congresswoman’s national favorability rating stood at just around 26 percent, with her unfavorable rating as high as 36 percent.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she told The Times. “And you don’t—and just in life in general—life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

As she weighs her options, Ocasio-Cortez said she is also considering her identity and how it may impact her chances. 

“I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina,” she said. “And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.”

Ocasio-Cortez made headlines over the summer with a series of candid Instagram posts announcing her decision to freeze her eggs. The decision drew backlash from Republicans, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who called the move a “political stunt.” 

Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris’ losses were also front of mind for Ocasio-Cortez.

“This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” she said. “That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism.”

Ocasio-Cortez told The Times that she had discussed a potential presidential campaign with Harris, who is also weighing a 2028 run, but declined to describe their conversations. 

The congresswoman also didn’t rule out challenging longtime New York senator Chuck Schumer, who has not announced whether he will run for reelection in 2028. 

Asked about whether she would still challenge Schumer if Democrats win back the Senate majority, Ocasio-Cortez said the decision wouldn’t “come down to deference.”

“Every element of this is something that’s within consideration,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

news.title: Trump-fueled gas prices, his ‘forever’ war and all those tariffs give Democrats a real shot at stealing this deep-red state
news.text:
On Monday, Rep. Ashley Hinson, President Donald Trump’s endorsed nominee in Iowa’s Senate race, made a public break from the president, calling for an end to the Iran War. 

That was surprising considering that just last week, before Speaker Mike Johnson dismissed the House of Representatives a day early, Hinson voted against a War Powers Act resolution to rein in Trump’s war. This came despite two of her Iowa Republican colleagues running for re-election — Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks — voting for the resolution.

But the pain at the gas tank is becoming too much across the board. 

Hence, she listed a series of policies to provide relief for Iowans, like pausing the gas tax and suspending exports of diesel fuel. 

“While doing this, we should also ensure our highway trust fund is replenished, so that Iowans don’t suffer from crumbling roads and bridges while relief comes our way now,” Hinson said. “These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”

In response, Josh Turek, the Paralympian-turned Democratic nominee for Senate, criticized Hinson for flip-flopping.

“You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week,” he posted on X. “It's time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first.”

But on Tuesday, Republicans’ reasons for breaking with Trump on Iran became clear. Marist University released a poll showing Turek besting Hinson by eight points. Lest anyone think that poll is an outlier, a YouGov poll showed Turek with a one-point lead in Iowa.

All of this seems to show that Iowa, which has undergone a political transformation in the past 15 years to become a staunchly Republican state, is prime for a Democratic takeover. 

For many Democrats, the last time they felt good about Iowa came in 2008 when Barack Obama turned his stunning win in the state’s presidential caucuses into winning the Hawkeye State by nine points in the general election. That same year, Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin would win his last term. Obama would win again in 2012 by just under 6 percentage points. 

But that would be the beginning of a long decline. In 2010, Republicans won the governorship and took over the state House of Representatives. In 2014, Harkin would retire and Joni Ernst would take over his seat. In 2016, Iowa would by more than 15 points to vote for Trump and Republicans would take control of the state senate.

Democrats would win three House seats in the 2018 midterm elections, only for Iowa to have an all-Republican delegation by 2022. Joe Biden would lose Iowa and Joni Ernst would win her re-election in 2020. 

But Trump has now taken a series of steps in Iowa that have put Republicans at risk in the state. For one, the war in Iran has caused the price of diesel fuel, which farmers use for tractors and other equipment, to skyrocket. According to AAA, the price of a gallon of diesel in the state is now $6.31 compared to $3.59 a year ago. 

There’s also the tariffs, which have put a massive strain on farmers. China has since pledged to purchase American-made soybeans, but it maintains a 10 percent tariff on American goods, including agricultural products. 

Another factor working in Democrats’ favor is the fact that Iowa’s unpopular Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds will not seek re-election. Most polls show the state’s Democratic Auditor Rob Sand beating Republican doctor Zach Lahn in the governor’s race. 

Of course, Democrats voters have every reason to not take these numbers at face value. Most famously, in 2024, Ann Selzer, the most respected pollster in Iowa, showed Kamala Harris with a three-point lead in the state against Trump in the final days before the election, only for him to mollywhop Harris by double digits. 

In addition, Hinson, while plenty conservative, has sought to portray herself as bipartisan and not a right-wing fire-breather on the issues. Republicans are also trying to recylce the issue of transgender athletes playing in women’s sports, even though Turek told NBC News and Sand told Politico that they oppose it. 

Lindsay James, who is running in Hinson’s old seat, for her part is running an ad saying “Parents know what's best for our kids. Washington needs to stay out of it.” 

But it’s not clear that hitting Democrats on transgender athletes will have the same salience in 2026 that it did in 2024, when Republicans messaged that Democrats cared more about cultural issues than they did the cost of living. Now, it’s the GOP that looks more focused on transgender people than the price of diesel and food. 

Iowa’s conservative lean might still save Hinson and some Republicans in the state. But if the top-ticket Republicans lose, they will have few people other than Trump to blame for losing a state that he had secured in their column for the past decade.
news.summary: A Republican Senate candidate is struggling to separate herself from Trump’s ‘forever wars,’ Eric Garcia writes. Democrats see an opening in that quandary
news.author: Eric Garcia

news.title: Susan Collins Blasted by Troy Jackson Over FBI Probe Report—‘Corruption’
news.text: Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, was hit with criticism from her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson after ProPublica published a report about her alleged interactions with a major campaign donor, as polls show a tight race in Maine six weeks out from the 2026 midterms. The FBI sought to launch a probe into Collins' dealings with a major donor, according to a ProPublica report, and the effort was abandoned after President Donald Trump's return to office, according to an investigation by the outlet. The report comes amid a tight Maine Senate race, one of the most competitive and closely watched contests in the 2026 midterms. Jackson responded to the report in a statement provided to Newsweek, accusing Collins of “corruption of the highest order.” “Susan Collins doesn’t care that we’re losing our health care, that ICE is killing people on the streets, and that we’ve been dragged into a pointless war—as long as her donors get their contracts and her coffers get filled. We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers,” he wrote. “The jig is up.” One Maine politics expert told Newsweek the report "could sting" Collins' reelection chances. Collins’ office denied the report in a statement to Newsweek. Annie Clark, who serves as Collins’ deputy chief of staff, said the claims in the report are “categorically false.” “There have never been any allegations of wrongdoing by the Collins for Senator campaign, and the campaign was never the target of the FBI investigation,” she wrote. Although Maine often leans Democratic and backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 7 points in 2024, Collins has been a longtime Republican powerhouse in the state. She has won by wide margins in the past due to her personal popularity and bipartisan image. Democrats have been hopeful about finally unseating Collins this year. The national environment appears favorable for a blue wave due to President Donald Trump’s falling national approval rating and economic concerns tied to inflation and the cost of living. While Collins has sought to distance herself from Trump, Jackson has painted her as being too close to the president in a state where Trump remains unpopular. What to Know About the FBI Anti-Corruption Probe into Susan Collins The ProPublica report focuses on alleged interactions between Collins and Martin Kao, the CEO of Navatek, a Hawaii-based military contractor. The report alleged that Scott Reed, a representative from her super PAC, met with the company executives to solicit a $500,000 donation. Government contractors are prohibited from making campaign contributions. The company’s CEO allegedly told Reed that Navatek “wanted Collins to guarantee tens of millions of dollars in additional federal funding,” ProPublica reported. An initial $150,000 donation was allegedly funneled to the PAC through a shell company, and he later told executives that Collins committed to securing $32 million in contracts for the company. He was indicted for making illegal campaign contributions in 2022 and told investigators about a wider effort involving Collins and other members of Congress—who were not named in the report—according to ProPublica. The publication noted Kao had “credibility issues.” Agents had asked for authorization to launch a bribery probe by late 2024. But when Trump returned to the White House, the investigation was effectively abandoned amid his administration’s sweeping changes to the FBI, the outlet reported. FBI Spokesperson Ben Williamson told ProPublica that the agency “ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign,” and nobody from her team has been charged. Susan Collins’ Office Rejects Report Clark said that ProPublica “took the word of someone who pled guilty to five counts of money laundering, three counts of wire fraud, one count of bank fraud, and making false submissions to the FEC.” “As Martin Kao was awaiting sentencing, he began making outlandish charges about the Collins office, deflecting blame from himself and placing it on Senator Collins, including alleging that our office required contributions before taking meetings and engaged in extortion, pay for play, and bribery,” she wrote. Clark also noted that the FBI and Court “obviously did not believe Kao,” pointing to his 2025 sentence in two separate cases, and that Collins’ campaign “cooperated fully” with the FBI during the investigation. She said the issues were resolved in 2021 and that the FBI has not contacted Collins about Kao ever since. What This Means for Midterms The report is a “pretty big deal,” Dan Shea, professor of political science at Colby College, told Newsweek. “For lots of split-ticket-voters Senator Collins makes sense because she delivers for the state. If that rationale is called into question—that she brings home federal funds in order to bolster her own campaign coffers—she will lose some of these voters,” he said. “Yeah, it could sting.” Moderate Democrats and unenrolled voters have been “key” to her past victories, he said. Her ability to bring home money to the state “trumps partisan leanings,” but that could be muddied by the report, he said. What Do Latest Polls Say About Susan Collins and Troy Jackson? Polls have shown a close race, with the latest survey from Quantus Insights showing a statistical tie, with Collins at 47.1 percent and Jackson at 46.4 percent. It surveyed 644 likely voters from September 14 to September 15, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.3 percentage points. Jackson, however, has held narrow leads in other polls. He was up 4 points in a YouGov poll, 48 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 1,378 registered voters from September 2 to September 8, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. A CNN poll showed Jackson up 3 points, 48 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 880 registered voters from August 31 to September 6, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. Jackson also led Collins by 2 points in a Fox News poll, 48 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,000 registered voters from August 6 to August 10, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research. Shea said the race is an “absolute toss up.” “Collins has more money and usually does better than the polls suggest. But Jackson will have a massive enthusiasm bubble on his side. I'd add that it looks like the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Hanna Pingree, will win easily. She's at the top of the ticket and that could help Jackson,” he said. Can Susan Collins Overcome National Headwinds? The race is expected to be close, and a Republican victory rests on Collins’ ability to withstand the national headwinds and hold onto support from independent voters and some moderate Democrats despite Trump’s poor national approval rating. But Republicans believe that if anyone is capable of winning in Maine this year, it would be Collins. Notably, the 2020 race between Collins and Democratic challenger Sara Gideon saw a notable polling error in Collins’ favor. Polling errors are not always duplicated from cycle to cycle, but a question about whether polls are slightly off this year continues to loom over the race. Maine is a tough state to poll due to its older, rural population. Collins trailed Gideon in nearly every poll but ultimately outperformed the polls to hold onto the seat, even as former President Joe Biden won the state by 9 points that year. Democrats are hopeful that a more blue environment will make Maine unwinnable for Collins, and Jackson, the former Maine Senate president, is viewed as a viable challenger, though Republicans have sought to cast him as too progressive for the more moderate state. The cycle has also been tumultuous for Democrats. Graham Platner, a progressive political newcomer whose campaign garnered national attention, was hit with sexual abuse allegations just weeks after clinching the Democratic nomination. He ultimately withdrew from the race but has denied the allegations. Jackson, who initially ran for governor but ultimately lost the primary, emerged as the new nominee during a convention in July, easily securing the required delegates to find his place on the ballot. Why Maine's Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms Democrats’ path to a Senate majority runs through Maine. Democrats are increasingly hopeful about winning the Senate despite a difficult map. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control if they win every race in a seat they currently hold. Vice President JD Vance serves as the tiebreaker in a split Senate. In order to flip the Senate majority, Democrats have to win every seat they currently hold, flip GOP-held seats in competitive states and win some seats in more traditionally conservative territory. Democrats are defending seats in Trump-won states Georgia and Michigan. In addition to Maine, they view a GOP-held seat in North Carolina as a top flip opportunity. The race in New Hampshire, which backed Harris by about 3 points, is also competitive. No other Senate races are in Harris-won or single-digit Trump states, meaning Democrats must expand the Senate battleground and compete in more conservative areas if they want to win the majority. They are targeting GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as potential states to flip. The Cook Political Report classifies those four races as tossups. What Happens Next Whether or not polls shift over the report could be seen over the coming weeks. Both candidates have agreed to face off in debates. Jackson’s campaign said the first debate could be held on October 6, and it would be hosted by WGME, a Portland-based news station. The race is considered a toss-up by forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Geoffrey Rowland.

news.title: Michigan AG Dana Nessel says she will vote for El-Sayed for Senate
news.text:
LANSING — Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said on a podcast aired Sept. 22 that she will vote for Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate, essentially giving her endorsement to a candidate who has split Michigan's Jewish community.

Nessel's endorsement of El-Sayed had been in doubt because she has expressed concerns about antisemitism in the Michigan Democratic Party and said she stayed away from the party's August nominating convention because she didn't feel safe. Many Michigan Jews have expressed reservation or opposition to El-Sayed for his criticism of the government of Israel and his refusal to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist as a Jewish state, among other reasons.

The race to fill the vacancy created by the pending retirement of U.S. Sen. Gary Peters is seen as a critical one for control of the U.S. Senate nationally.

El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman from White Lake Township.

"I don't want to say the choice is easy, but I am going to say there is no choice," Nessel, a Democrat who is Jewish, said on the Michigan podcast "For the Sake of the Argument," hosted by Lori Goldman.

"We have one candidate that I know is going to fight against the Trump administration, is going to protect both our physical security, our safety, our health, our futures. And then we have another candidate, Mike Rogers, who's not going to do any of that," Nessel said.

She said one of Rogers' primary concerns is "how many pats on the back he can get from (Republican President) Donald Trump."

El-Sayed, appearing on the same podcast, told Nessel he was grateful for her support.

"I'm particularly grateful for it because I know we haven't always agreed on everything," he said.

Nessel endorsed El-Sayed's opponent, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, in the Democratic primary.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democratic nominee for president, also endorsed El-Sayed for U.S. Senate while campaigning with him in Detroit Sept. 22, according to a Fox 2 video feed of the event. Harris said at a roundtable related to reproductive justice and Black maternal health that El-Sayed would be a strong voice for Michigan and the nation.

Free Press staff writer Clara Hendrickson contributed to this report.

news.text:
DSA leads the blue wave — will it bend to the thin blue line?
by Mansa Musa, The Real News Network September 22, 2026

https://youtu.be/CR9Aywg_6Tw

What will a DSA-led state look like — will it back defund and community control of police, or bow to the powers that block affordability? Lawrence Grandpre, political commentator for Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle, explores this question in his recent Baltimore Times article, "The Dangers of 'Law and Order' Leftism: Toward a Black Power Public Safety," asking whether DSA will embrace the outmoded Law and Order politics that fueled America's prison boom. As officials like AOC and Mamdani backtrack on defunding police — one of the biggest carceral drains on housing, healthcare, and education funding — Grandpre sits down with former political prisoner and Rattling the Bars host Mansa Musa to unpack these contradictions ahead of the midterms, where Democrats hope to retake the House and Senate. Tune in for an unflinching look at the Left's relationship to the state and to law and order.
Related Links:

The Dangers of “Law and Order” Leftism- Toward a Black Power Public Safety
Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle Facebook, X, Instagram, Bluesky, LinkedIn, Youtube

Production/Post-production: Cameron Granadino

The following is a rushed transcript and may contain errors. It will be updated.
Mansa Musa:
Welcome to Rattling the Bars. I'm your host Mansa Musa. Today I'm joined by Lance Grandpre, political commentator with Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle, to discuss his recent article for Baltimore Times, "The Dangers of 'Law and Order' Leftism—Toward a Black Power Public Safety." Thank you for joining me, Lance.
Lawrence Grandpre:
Thank you for having me.
Mansa Musa:
Alright, so let's start like this here. At one point we had in 2020 where you had a push for the abolishment of prisons and to dismantle the police system as we see it during that period. But immediately you had a pushback and the pushback came in the form of saying that this was woke. Now we look at the United States and mass incarceration, armed policing, and you juxtapose that with the lack of funds for healthcare, lack of funds for education and lack of funds for housing and the fact that the criminal injustice system is in itself painful when it comes to poor and oppressed people, mainly people of color. Let's start with your article.
Lawrence Grandpre:
So this article stems out of a protest I went to because sometimes people say if you talk about police reform or defunding police, you don't care about victims. And this protest was the opposite. This was a Black elder, a former member of the Baltimore Black Panther Party who was assaulted by many teenagers and it was caught on film. So of course Fox News, our local Fox News is showing this over and over again saying, "Lock them up, what's wrong with these kids?" And these were community advocates, many of them women, Queen Mother Victorious who lost her son to gun violence, Mama Gwen, who was formerly incarcerated, coming together with community and saying these young people, what they did was a problem, not because it just violated the law, because it violated our community respect for elders. And we don't want to just throw the cops at these kids and throw away the book, but if people know who these young people are, turn them into us, the Black community, so we can make sure that they are held accountable but not railroaded by the criminal legal system.
And I though the sophistication and intelligence of that response and even Baba Ade, the elder who was hurt, saying the Black Panther's argument was that capitalism and racism breed criminality in the community.
Mansa Musa:

Lawrence Grandpre:
And it's not for us as the vanguard to educate ourselves and use political consciousness to eliminate criminality, not just from a material standpoint, but from a psycho-spiritual standpoint. And it was really interesting because this was a few days after AOC went on the news and said, "Nobody's talking about defund anymore. Woke 1.0 was crazy." So it was really interesting that the people who were supposed to be talking about social justice, Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez, some of these other so-called leftists,
Mansa Musa:

Lawrence Grandpre:
Even they were saying, "Defund—that was just people on Twitter trying to look woke. Nobody really talks about defund in real life." And these Black elders, Black people in West Baltimore, were saying things like, "We have a $700 million police budget in Baltimore. How are we going to have that and schools and investments in the Black youth?" So these Black people who the left is telling us are conservative are actually more progressive than the DSA.
And I thought that was very telling that, in this moment, going into the midterms, there are these leftist democratic socialists who are trying to get elected, and because they want to get elected, they want to push away from radical rhetoric because they think it's turning off voters. And I think that that goes to show you that when it comes to Black people, we need to have our own vision of public safety, because what's being offered by even the left, the Democratic Socialists, is willing to push our issues aside, because they have a misunderstanding of our issues. They think it's just a bunch of radicals on Twitter as opposed to Black folks been talking about Defund since the '50s. And our visions of Defund are very different than what you saw on Twitter in 2020, but these folks wouldn't know that.
Mansa Musa:
So how do you see the DSA in terms of how they look at the budget, just police budget and the fact that it's undercutting the services of the very people they supposed to be representing?
Lawrence Grandpre:
It's interesting because I think if you are a democratic socialist, it's obvious you believe police are a tool to protect capitalism. So a world where if you're a socialist, the idea that you wouldn't talk about [how] protecting capitalism getting more money is a problem for you—it's weird.
Mansa Musa:

Lawrence Grandpre:
But these folks are a particular brand of socialist. Many of them were very much pro-Bernie Sanders. So when Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris used conversations about identity to attack Bernie, now a lot of these folks see all conversations about race as just distraction from class issues.
So, even when Black people talk about police, they say, "Well, it's not serious. No one really talks about Defund. So you're really just trying to attack the socialist candidates." And it's like, no, Black folks have been the community control of the police platform.
It wasn't just invented by the Black Panther Party. It was talked about by Black activists in the '40s and '50s, in part because the understanding that if the police were seen as a solution to all social problems... it's not just police, it's police-ism: the idea that policing is the only solution to the problems facing all poor people, but especially Black poor people, that's going to push money away from all the other programs we need in the Black community. So Black folks have been saying that, really, since the Northern migration.
So when we talk about community control of the police, part of that is having community control boards control the police themselves, hold them accountable. And we've worked on that as LBS, but it's also community control of the institutions that produce public safety beyond police. So, housing, addiction, education. I mean, I love to point out that Bobby Seal, he was in AmeriCorps before he was a Panther. So he would be shooting dice with the Black kids trying to school them on AmeriCorps' time. And part of his frustration is these nonprofits don't let us actually do the training we need to do with these youth, but we got to get the money from the nonprofit because that's the only job we got. So even the Black Panthers program was a push for Black control of resources to socialize our youth, specifically around things like violence prevention. And again, the idea that all of that is just under this large framework of "woke"... And again, the right wing hates woke, we know that, but even some of the Bernie folks—they really hate "woke," because they associate it with the attacks on Bernie and they see all conversations about police as woke.
Mansa Musa:
Let's unpack some more about DSA because we see upheaval of DSA type activity and we see in terms of midterm elections, some of the candidates that ran on DSA platform have made it through the primary. And so at the same token, what is their appeal? Because they vacillating when it come to social issues.
Lawrence Grandpre:
The federal government, in theory, can print money. So there's this belief that if we just spent more money, things will get better, and the Democrats have been afraid to spend money. I think that in the DSA, it's like, "Let's really focus on, in theory, cut the military budget, invest in community through things like Medicare for Al"l. Now, if you don't have the integrity to stand up for "Defund the Police," why do you think we would believe that you have the integrity to stand up to "Cut the Military Budget? If you don't see the connections between the violence of policing and the violence of militarism, why would we expect you to be able to push the military budget to community?" 
Lawrence Grandpre:
These are intelligent, college-educated voters who feel like the government needs to spend more money, in part, because it's a job program for people like them. So they have an interest in fighting the austerity of the Democratic Party, in part, because they want to see conditions improve for the community, but also in part because it's a business model for the voters of DSA. And that's a big concern for us, because even with Medicare for All, there's no world in which healthcare should be a for-profit enterprise. But it's not just that doctors are racist. When you look at things like Black women get more cesarean sections than other women, So, literally, they're getting cut open in these dangerous surgeries. Black women, if you have a child in the hospital, you are going to get a drug test. And even if you pop for that drug test from the epidural, the drugs they give you for the pain, they might take your kid away. So engagements with the medical system are not just imperfect for Black people; they are places of surveillance and violence.
So we, as Black people, need systems like a birthing center, like nutrition, upstream investments that are different than what the DSA crowd cares about. So the idea that we should just accept not talking about Defund to get Medicare for All ignores the fact that Black people—we don't just need healthcare to not give us a bill. We need to change the vision of healthcare so we control it. And the DSA is not interested in that. They don't really think that way. And they honestly believe the only way anything will get passed if it goes to everybody. Universal programs prevent racial backlash. Because we know any spending in America is seen as giving money to welfare queens. So we just got to give the same thing to everybody and that'll deal with racial backlash.
And what we know is anything you do that gives out any tax money will deal with racial backlash, but also do things that don't give Black people the power we need to build for ourselves. It will just put us in systems that really are built by other people that, even if it's good for them, can often be violent for us.
Lawrence Grandpre:
But I think that, again, when you have a class-based vision of the world, that has become in some ways hostile to thinking about race because you had negative experiences with people weaponizing race against people like Bernie Sanders. You're not thinking about what a political agenda would look like when you actually invest in... because we should do both. We should have a class-based redistribution of wealth, but that restribution should also be invested in community institutions that reflect the culture and history of specific communities, not just Medicare for All, but clinics that use the history and culture of the community to provide that healthcare. Nutrition that reflects the culture and the way communities like to be fed so that they can have upstream nutrition so they don't need to go to the doctor in the first place.
These things should go hand in hand. And I think it's concerning that it feels like, because DSA is becoming electorally viable in some spaces, that [they] only talk about affordability issues, only talk about Medicare for all, only talk about ending the war in Iran, without really thinking intelligently about a platform that would meet people's needs for community control of public safety, broadly defined. So not just policing, but again, youth programming, schooling, getting nutrition. Our kids are literally hungry.
Mansa Musa:

Lawrence Grandpre:
They're fed junk food, but they're undernourished. So we actually do have serious nutritional needs as we have obesity in the inner city. news.title: AOC opens up about race, gender in weighing possible 2028 White House bid
news.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., raised concerns during an interview published Tuesday about how her race and gender could factor into a potential 2028 presidential bid. "Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ocasio-Cortez said in an interview with The New York Times. "I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities." The progressive congresswoman said of a possible White House run, "I think about it personally." "I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life," she added. AOC, ASKED ABOUT RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS HER AMBITION IS 'WAY BIGGER THAN THAT' "This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?" she told the Times. "That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism." Ocasio-Cortez said the discussion around race and gender was often seen as a complaint or excuse. "I often hesitate to even talk about it," she told the outlet, "because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint." "If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh," she told the Times of possibly running for president. "It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?" HASAN PIKER BRUSHES OFF DEMS WHO SEE HIM AS A LIABILITY, NAMES HIS '28 CHOICE She argued people get defensive when gender is suggested as playing a role in electoral politics. "I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left," she told the Times. Ocasio-Cortez has been generating 2028 buzz. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman described the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic." Hoffman made the comments at Politico's Decoded Summit in September, and said former Vice President Kamala Harris would have a "very challenging path" to the nomination. "It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for." AOC’S PRIMARY WIN REIGNITES SPECULATION OVER 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SCHUMER CHALLENGE Far-left streamer Hasan Piker said he would absolutely campaign for AOC should she decide to run in 2028. Ocasio-Cortez topped a July poll from the University of New Hampshire Granite State. In the poll, AOC was one point ahead of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and 17 points ahead of Harris. The polling average as of Sept. 22, according to the New York Times, has Harris leading with 27%, followed by Gov. Gavin Newsom at 16%, Buttigieg with 10%, and Ocasio-Cortez also at 10%. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Judy Pino, advisor on Hispanic issues and a Spanish-language spokesperson for Independent Women and The LIBRE Initiative, reacted to Ocasio-Cortez' remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital. Pino said, "Whether America is ready for a Latina president isn’t the question. As a Latina, I find that framing beside the point and, frankly, insulting." "It reduces a serious debate about the future of this country to gender and ethnicity when Americans are worried about whether they can afford groceries, buy a home, grow a business, and create a better future for their children," she continued. Pino said Ocasio-Cortez "identifies" with democratic socialism, and argued, "we should believe candidates when they tell us what they stand for." "For many Latinos, that debate has particular resonance. Families from Cuba, Venezuela and elsewhere in Latin America have witnessed governments embrace socialism while expanding state control and restricting economic and political freedom. Those experiences help explain why the word ‘socialism’ can carry consequences far beyond a political slogan for some Latino families,' Pino said in the statement. Pino said Latino voters were more focused on AOC's policies rather than her gender or ethnicity. "That's the debate America should be having: not whether we're ready for a Latina president, but whether Americans want to move this country in a socialist direction," she said.
news.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., opened up about how race and gender factor into her 2028 presidential election calculus in a new interview.
