news.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on 2028: ‘Life doesn’t wait for you to be ready’
news.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., has said she will weigh the decision of whether to run for president after the midterm elections. The decision is clearly already weighing on her.

In an interview with The New York Times, Ocasio-Cortez revealed the electoral equations she is crunching and the mental “math” she is calculating as she approaches the biggest crossroads of her political career.

Her gender. Her ethnicity. Her electability. Her eggs. Her movement. Her moment.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she said. “And you don’t — and just in life in general — life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

Ocasio-Cortez, 36, the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, is now in her eighth year representing parts of the Bronx and Queens. She could simply keep winning reelection. But in 2028, she has two other choices: run for the White House or seek the seat now held by Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York.

“Every element of this is something that’s within consideration,” she said.

Ocasio-Cortez weighed aloud the pros and cons of running for president with unusual candor, sounding less strategic than searching, as if the right answer were somewhere nearby.

At times, she played the part of political pundit handicapping her own potential presidential candidacy from afar. At others, she voiced the unvarnished concerns of a woman who just opened up on Instagram (“Bloat check!”) about fertility treatments preparing for a possible future pregnancy.

“I think about it personally,” she said of a White House run. “I am 36; I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life.”

“Pretty candidly, I think about my identity,” Ocasio-Cortez went on. “I’m not naive to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.”

Ocasio-Cortez arrived in Congress as a left-wing outsider and remains one of the party’s most progressive voices. Some party strategists are urging Democrats to move to the middle. But Ocasio-Cortez was heartened by “the ascendance for the first time” of progressives like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan who toppled big-money candidates in this year’s Senate primaries.

“I have a tremendous amount of fear over the corruption of our political system,” she said.

She spoke by phone last week as she recovered in her Washington apartment from COVID-19. She had called to discuss an upcoming swing through upstate New York and a cash transfer to help Democrats in her home state.

She wound up describing much more.

‘Everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?’

Ocasio-Cortez knows that broaching the roles of race and gender in politics can be unpopular, even unappealing. “I often hesitate to even talk about it,” she said, “because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint.”

She is talking about it anyway.

“If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh,” she said of running for president as a woman. “It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?”

She described the gender gap as a fact of American electoral politics: Roughly 27% of Congress is female, she said, and zero percent of past presidents.

It’s not just that a five-second video of her adjusting her hair in the Bronx this year drew more than 25 million views on social platform X and a tsunami of sexualized replies (“that’s the most kind of, like, brazen and obvious forms of it,” she said). It’s how “female politicians are discussed, approached, covered” overall.

“What is very odd about our political culture is that for some reason when you raise it, people just freak out,” she said. “They get so defensive at the mere suggestion that gender could play a role.”

She made plain that this was a problem “independent of ideology.”

“I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left,” she said.

The losses of the only two women ever to secure the Democratic presidential nomination, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, loom large. “It may or may not be related, but I absolutely empathize with the heartbreak that people feel around that and, frankly, how those women were treated,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

She said she had discussed the issue with Harris, who is also considering a 2028 run, but she declined to describe their private conversations.

“This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” Ocasio-Cortez said with a laugh. “That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism.”

Little desire for ‘deference’

Few politicians can command public attention like Ocasio-Cortez. Her egg-freezing set off a national conversation about fertility. Her offhand remark on ABC News that “Woke one was crazy” spawned a thousand takes on her thinking and her party’s evolution.

No matter the size of her megaphone, it is also true that no House member has ascended directly to the presidency in modern history. (Few see any applicable lessons in the election of James A. Garfield in 1880.) Even if she is one of the House’s most prolific fundraisers, a potential attempted leap to the White House would be essentially unprecedented.

The Senate seat in New York could be an alluring alternative.

Ocasio-Cortez, who won her seat by toppling a powerful Democratic House leader in a 2018 primary, did not rule out the possibility of challenging Schumer — even if he helps Democrats win a Senate majority in the midterms.

“That would honestly be the best possible problem we could have as a country,” she said of the idea that a Democratic Senate majority could further complicate her 2028 choices. She added, “We’re working hard to have that problem, and I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.”

Schumer, 75, has not announced his own 2028 plans.

Ocasio-Cortez made this much clear: She is not waiting on anyone other than herself, whether that pits her as a primary challenger to a potential Senate majority leader or to a former vice president.

“I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference,” she said.

Why a White House run would be ‘very all or nothing’

Back in May, Ocasio-Cortez went viral for an answer she gave at a forum with David Axelrod, the onetime adviser to former President Barack Obama, in which she said her ambitions were not a “title or a seat.”

“My ambition is way bigger than that,” she said. “My ambition is to change this country. Presidents come and go; Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go, but single-payer healthcare is forever; a living wage is forever; workers’ rights are forever, women’s rights, all of that.”

Axelrod said in an interview that he believed Ocasio-Cortez when she spoke about her motivations.

“She is very honest in her communications. It’s what makes her disarming,” he said. “Her bottom line is producing something for the people she’s fighting for, so I think this decision is partly seen through that prism.”

In her interview with the Times, Ocasio-Cortez repeated variations of that line about her lack of interest in “my title.” But she also expressed a keen awareness of the realities that House members must seek reelection every two years and that losing would mean being out of office entirely.

“It’s very all or nothing,” she said. “If I were to run in this cycle, and not win, I would be done.

“And I am not opposed to that,” she added. But it was also a consideration. “That, in and of itself, does not exclude the decision,” she finally said. “But it has to make it worth it.”

A successor to Bernie Sanders?

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., her mentor and ally, is 85. Many on the left see Ocasio-Cortez as his natural successor. The two politicians’ “Fighting Oligarchy” tour in 2025 drew huge crowds.

“These rallies were bigger than the sum of their parts,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “When Bernie was on his own, or when I’m on my own, it’s different because we have overlapping but also complementary coalitions.”

In other words, she is thinking about the political coalition of Sanders, the runner-up in the last two open Democratic presidential primaries — and how it might intersect with her own.

Sanders had advantages that Ocasio-Cortez does not. His 2016 run made him a national figure on the left before the right took to attacking him. Ocasio-Cortez has been a boogeywoman for Republicans almost since her arrival on the scene in 2018, and she would be the Democratic Party’s most progressive standard-bearer in decades, if not ever.

In a recent New York Times/Siena University poll, her favorable rating among Republicans was less than 1% — with 75% rating her unfavorably.

Overall, just 30% of likely voters nationally viewed her favorably, with 41% holding an unfavorable opinion.

Her democratic socialist ally, Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York City, had a higher favorable rating, 38%, and a lower unfavorable rating, 33%. (Born in Uganda, Mamdani is not eligible to serve as president.)

Ocasio-Cortez hailed Mamdani, 34, as “an incredible political talent.”

“There are also major differences between an executive position for a municipal seat and a legislative position,” she said, which regularly sets up “conflict with your peers.”

“Of course, obviously, there are …” she paused. “I don’t know why it’s controversial to say that there are headwinds in identity and gender.”

Ocasio-Cortez is not just a good fundraiser. She has raised $32 million from January 2025 to July 2026 — more than double the sum that any other House incumbent raised in their reelection account other than Speaker Mike Johnson or Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader.

She is prideful of her almost exclusive dependence on small donors.

“I have a tremendous amount of fear over the corruption of our political system,” she said. “There’s very few people who are financially independent from special interests that are able to advocate directly for the needs of working people.”

In the end, Ocasio-Cortez landed on the most familiar of lines to describe the driving force behind her 2028 decision.

“Where can I do the most good?”

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Trump’s war with the press has finally met some resistance

The Trump Show has always needed the press, but on Donald’s terms. This time around, the press is finally saying no.

7.01pm, 22 Sep 2026

Share options

Marion McKeone

BY THE TIME you read this column, it is entirely possible that CNN, MS Now and Politico, the three news outlets that were banned by Trump last Friday, will be back at their White House media perches, lobbing questions and being ignored or excoriated as fake news/dumb/corrupt/lousy journalists who are (in the case of female journalists only) ‘ugly on the inside and out’.

It’s also possible that Trump will have pulled the plug on the entire White House TV pool, casting out Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC for having the temerity to stand up for their CNN colleagues by refusing to provide camera and sound crews for Trump’s events on Monday.

After almost a decade of belittling its members and whittling away its First Amendment rights, the White House press corps has finally grown the semblance of a spine with its first unified defiance of the White House authoritarian creep that has long since progressed to a gallop.

The TV pool’s refusal to step into the breach caused by Trump’s banning of CNN, the fifth member of the White House TV pool, was followed by a refusal by the New York Times, the Washington Post, Associated Press and other outlets to publish photographs of Trump’s scheduled appearances on Monday. His meeting with New York Mayor Zohran Mandami, his visit to the UN General Assembly and his meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron were subjected to a visual blackout, although smaller entities picked up the slack.

A moment of unintentional comedic gold transpired when the White House comms team attempted to plug the gap by providing their own footage of Trump cutting the ribbon around his brand-new White House helicopter pad. But someone forgot to wire him for sound; as a result, the footage is accompanied by incoherent emissions from the US President.

Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

The cynic in me says the White House press corps’ united stance stems from the near-certain knowledge that this battle over access will be brief and relatively bloodless. Media coverage is oxygen for the reality TV President, and with Xi Jinping dropping by for a cup of tea later this week, it’s unthinkable that Trump would allow the Chinese leader to witness his television pool’s revolution.

Advertisement

The court will likely ride to his rescue before XI’s plane touches down, neutralising the consequences of his temper tantrum. CNN, MS Now and Politico promptly sued Trump, and an initial hearing is scheduled to take place tomorrow (Wednesday) afternoon before District Judge Tim Kelly, who gave short shrift to Trump’s 2018 attempt to strip CNN reporter Jim Acosta of his White House hard pass.

Back then Kelly felt no need to broach weighty First Amendment issues. Instead, he issued a narrow ruling that found that Acosta’s Fifth Amendment rights to due process had been trampled. He stipulated that should a future President feel the urge to cast out any – or indeed all – of the 495 reporters who currently hold hard passes, he must first provide advance written notice of his reason for doing so and provide the target of his ire with an opportunity to formally challenge the decision.

Neither of those happened before Trump’s decided to ban more than 100 reporters, editors, producers and camera crew from CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House last Friday.

Following the law

Hard passes can only be revoked if the journalist is deemed to represent a verified security threat to the President or his family, or if they fail to meet normal behavioural standards. A fistfight in the Oval Office, for example, or ingesting drugs in the Press Room would be considered reasonable grounds for ejecting a reporter. Asking tough questions or publishing a critical analysis of a policy decision would not. So even if Trump had followed the procedural steps laid out by Kelly last weekend, there is no substantive reason behind his decision.

That the White House press corps has finally joined together in defence of their colleagues is laudable. That it has taken them more than a decade to do so is utterly shameful. Their representative body, the White House Press Correspondents Association (WHCA) – and I say this as a former member – is amongst the most spineless of any Washington DC-based organisation.

The WHCA hasn’t just stood by in silence as Trump insulted, humiliated and berated its members for having the temerity to do their jobs. It has abdicated even its most basic duties – allowing former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt to annex its right to select White House pool members and even remove its right to allocate the 49 seats in the White House press room to journalists according to seniority and outlet reach, allowing Trump to stack the press room with right-wing influencers and pass over veteran journalists in favour of MAGA know-nothings who can be relied upon to offer praise and platitudes instead of questions.

Last year AP, a global news agency whose coverage reaches an estimated four billion people worldwide, was dropped from the White House pool and banned from the Oval Office and Air Force One because it declined to parrot Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. As an international news organisation, its decision was entirely correct. AP has also sued the White House. That case focuses on the narrower question of whether a major media outlet can be excluded from a White House pool of about 20 members.

Trump’s latest overreach is unsurprising, given how much ground the White House media has already ceded. Since 2015, it has placated, flattered, justified, equivocated and, under the pretext of ‘even-handedness’, bestowed a false equivalence between Trump and his Democratic rivals. This has resulted in contorted efforts to fashion the morally asymmetric into the symmetric, comparing Hillary Clinton’s misuse of a private email server with Trump’s mendacity, sexual misconduct, lack of political experience and dubious business practices. Or the 2024 equation of his attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 election with Kamala Harris’s failure to disavow Joe Biden’s economic policies. 

The Trump Show

Lest the prospect of a break in the daily fire hose of Trump-adulation masquerading as media coverage induce a premature case of delirium tremens, never fear. Trump TV: The Essentials Station was launched on Monday night at 7 pm Washington DC time.

The promise to Make Television Great Again is underscored by a 24-hour streaming platform of all things Trump, which will operate 7 days a week. How precisely it will use its own airwaves is not yet clear. Even Trump, for all his uncanny ability to insert himself front and centre of every American and international news story, may have a hard time generating new controversies around the clock.

The answer may be in the title – Trump; Essentials sounds like one of those greatest hits-adjacent ‘filler’ albums put out by 1980s artists that are short on hits and long on B-sides. Which means we’ll get to revisit what Trump regards as his greatest political triumphs on a loop – untroubled by reality, much less fact-checkers.

And so we’ll likely be treated to reprises of Trump being feted with swords in Saudi Arabia, Trump striding across global stages shoving minions out of his path, Trump yukking it up with Kim Jung Un, Putin and Xi Jinping.

And expect plenty of Trump ‘fight fight fight’ reruns from Butler, Pennsylvania, along with the rapturous welcomes he’s received at the 2016, 2020 and 2024 RNC conventions – interspersed with the Fifa accolade for the eight wars he ended – in his own head at least. The war he started is unlikely to feature prominently.

White House Press Corps or not, the Trump show will continue.

news.title: James Talarico Sees 28-Point Swing in Texas Trump Stronghold: Private Poll
news.text: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has seen a massive 28-point swing in vote share in Texas State Senate District 9, compared to President Donald Trump's numbers in 2024, according to a new private poll acquired by Harvey Kronberg’s Quorum Report. The turnaround is another sign that Republicans are, for the first time since 1988, seriously in danger of losing a Senate race in the state. Talarico, a Democratic state lawmaker, is facing off against Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated incumbent GOP Senator John Cornyn in May to secure his party’s nomination after gaining Trump’s endorsement in the bitterly fought contest. Democrats are hoping to ride a blue wave into the majority in both the House and Senate in November so that they can dramatically restrict Trump’s ability to pass legislation in the final two years of his second term. Internal Poll On Monday, the Quorum Report published what it called an internal Republican poll showing Talarico with 52 percent of the vote in Texas State Senate District 9. Paxton had 41 percent, giving Talarico an 11-point lead. In 2024, Trump defeated Democratic nominee Kamala Harris by 17 points in the district, so the internal poll reveals a huge 28-point move away from the GOP compared to the last presidential election. Texas State Senate District 9 includes areas of Tarrant County, including a sizable chunk of Fort Worth. The polling numbers comes after the district was already the site of a huge political upset in January when Democrat Taylor Rehmet beat Republican Leigh Wambsganss by over 14 points in a special election, the first time the district had voted blue since 1991. The poll of 600 likely voters in the district was conducted between September 10 and September 15 and had a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points. Quorum Report noted that, unusually, they had published the results of a poll “without revealing how we got the numbers and without publishing the polling memo.” The outlet added, “It’s not our usual MO [modus operandi] and it frustrates professional pollsters. When to do it, it’s a judgement call, for sure. We’re doing it again today but not without first offering a prime example of how it can help your understanding of the shape of a campaign.” General Polling Last week, Talarico led Paxton in eight different polls, the first time he led with all of those pollsters, as an Emerson College survey conducted between September 12 and September 14 gave the Democrat a one-percentage-point lead, 47 percent to the attorney general’s 46 percent. A new Siena College/ReconMR poll published on Thursday, conducted from September 8 to September 11, put Talarico ahead of Paxton with 49 percent of the vote to 43 percent. Talarico has become the favorite on both Kalshi and Polymarket prediction markets. Kalshi gives Talarico a 59 percent chance of victory, versus 41 percent for Paxton, while Polymarket puts the Democrat at 62 percent versus just 39 percent for his GOP rival. The numbers come as both sides ramp up fundraising. According to Federal Election Commission filings, Paxton recently received another $5 million from MAGA Inc., the main pro-Trump political action committee. Controversial Candidate Paxton has long been controversial even within Texas Republican circles and was impeached in 2023 by the GOP-dominated Texas House after being accused of misuse of power, though he was later acquitted by the state Senate. In May, an endorsement from Trump helped push Paxton past the finish line against Cornyn in the Republican primary. Cronyn had been in the Senate since 2002. news.title: Nearly Three-In-Four Democrats Indicate They’re Comfortable With The Military Overthrowing Donald Trump
news.text:
A new poll shows that 72 percent of Democrats would either support or have no opinion regarding a military coup against President Donald Trump to “safeguard the Constitution,” as a similar number say that he should be criminally prosecuted.

Conducted by the Center for Strategic Politics in collaboration with Liberal Currents, Monday’s poll asked 683 Democratic voters a range of questions regarding their ideal next steps for American politics. (RELATED: Defamation Case Ruling Supports Claim That Dems’ Star J6 Witness Lied Under Oath)

One question asked how Democrats would respond to waking up to news of one of several scenarios in which Trump is no longer in office.

Of those asked, 86 percent said that they would have positive feelings if Trump were impeached and convicted by Congress and removed from office. Another 84 percent said that they would feel positive about hearing that Trump’s Cabinet used the 25th Amendment to declare the president unfit for office and remove him.

Another 56 percent said that they would feel positive upon hearing that Trump had died overnight in his sleep, and another 31 percent said that they would feel positive about hearing that Trump was assassinated while speaking at a rally.

Additionally, 59 percent of Democrats said that they would feel positive about hearing that a group of U.S. military leaders had removed Trump from power before assuming control of the U.S. in order to “safeguard the Constitution.” Another 13 percent said they would have neither a positive nor a negative opinion. Only 28 percent said that they would have a negative reaction to Trump being removed from office by the military. 

We polled five routes for Trump to leave office before the end of his term. A plurality of Dems support four of them, including a military coup and death by natural causes. The only one underwater, an assassination, is still supported by 29%. pic.twitter.com/C3qb2H0R8j— Center for Strategic Politics (@StratPolitics) September 21, 2026

Another question asked Democrats if their next administration should pursue criminal prosecution for a range of actions taken by the current administration.

Of those asked, 77 percent said members of Trump’s administration should be held criminally accountable for actions taken by immigration and border enforcement, and 73 percent said that the White House’s homeland security adviser, Stephen Miller, should be prosecuted for his actions involving such enforcement.

Another 72 percent said the administration should be prosecuted for its lethal strikes on boats trafficking drugs to the U.S. in South America, and 57 percent said that members of both the Trump and Biden administrations should be prosecuted for “actions taken related to Israel’s genocide in Gaza.”

For actions taken prosecuting the War in Iran, 66 percent of Democrats said that the administration should be prosecuted, while 69 percent said that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth should face criminal charges for “his role in directing the US military to violate national and international law.”

Criminal prosecutions of Trump officials are generally favored by Dems, with clear majorities indicating support in all cases. Voters also support prosecution of officials from both the Trump and Biden admins over US support for Israel's genocide in Gaza. pic.twitter.com/OF6tRVasF8— Center for Strategic Politics (@StratPolitics) September 21, 2026

So, who would Democrats rather have in office today?

When asked how favorable they were of left-wing public figures, 70 percent said they viewed Vice President Kamala Harris favorably, 66 percent said they viewed California Gov. Gavin Newsom favorably, and another 70 percent said they viewed former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg favorably.

In contrast, The New York Times places Trump’s overall approval rating at only 37 percent as of Tuesday. (RELATED: Republicans Getting Fed Up With Trump’s Iran Project, Poll Shows)

Additionally, a majority of Democrats said that they would support packing the Supreme Court, accepting more immigrants, and the end of the filibuster.

news.title: Can Kamala Harris repair Michigan’s 2024 fractures?
news.text:
DETROIT — To hear Abdul El-Sayed tell it, the 2024 election left Michigan Democrats with several kinds of pain.

There was the pain of a party divided over Gaza, with some voters feeling betrayed by the Democratic Party’s leadership. The pain of Kamala Harris’ loss to Donald Trump. And the pain of the blame that followed.

With 42 days until the midterms, El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate, is enlisting Harris herself to help the party heal, or at least move on.

“I was very clear that I disagreed with my party when it came to the genocide. I was very clear that I disagreed with my party when it comes to funding a foreign military unconditionally,” El-Sayed told reporters Tuesday at a press conference.

But he acknowledged another kind of pain too.

“There was a lot of pain from folks who said, ‘Look, we should have avoided Donald Trump, we could have avoided Donald Trump. We would be in a better position on everything from gas to groceries to Gaza if Donald Trump was not the president right now,’” he said.

On Tuesday the former vice president will campaign in Michigan for the first time since her 2024 defeat. She is lending her status as one of the party’s most prominent national figures to boost El-Sayed as he works to consolidate support among Black Michiganders in the closing weeks of his Senate race.

The visit will be Harris' second appearance in a battleground state on behalf of a midterm candidate. It’s the first of a series of scheduled fall general election campaign events by Harris. She will stump for Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia at the end of October and return to Nevada to campaign for Aaron Ford, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee.

Harris will first join El-Sayed for a roundtable on maternal and infant mortality. The issue disproportionately affects Black women, and she made it a feature of her 2024 platform. Afterward, she will hold a fireside chat with Black state leaders, including the Rev. Dr. Wendell Anthony, the longtime president of the Detroit branch of the NAACP.

El-Sayed has spent months courting Black voters on his own. He has made regular visits to predominantly Black churches, and last week he released a slate of policy proposals aimed at expanding access to capital for Black-owned businesses and building affordable housing in Black communities.

Still, El-Sayed and several Black Democratic leaders in Michigan told MS NOW that the clearest benefit of Harris' visit may be its potential to ease, and perhaps repair, tensions between the state's Black and Arab American communities. Those tensions predate 2024, they said. But they deepened after anger over U.S. military aid to Israel led many Arab American voters in Michigan to withhold their support from Harris. She lost the state to Trump, and she also lost the Arab-majority city of Dearborn.

El-Sayed and several leaders of the 2024 Uncommitted movement, including co-founder Abbas Alawieh, ultimately backed Harris. But some voters still remember their early opposition, and it has colored how they see El-Sayed. That was especially true after Rep. Haley Stevens, his rival in the Democratic primary, repeatedly highlighted his history. One ad accused him of "disrespecting women," Harris among them.

The attack stuck. Stevens won more than 60% of Black voters in the primary, some of whom specifically cited El-Sayed's support for the Uncommitted movement as a reason they didn't back him. 

That, El-Sayed told MS NOW, is what sets his race apart from those of other candidates the former vice president has endorsed who have sought to distance their campaigns from her, including Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola and Iowa's Josh Turek, another Senate candidate.

“There were some hurt feelings about the engagement with the Arab and Muslim community around the 2024 election. Folks saying, ‘Well, if your community couldn't stand up for Vice President Harris, why should we stand up with you?’" El-Sayed told MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.” “Even though I was on the right side of that conversation, but who better to say it than Vice President Harris.”

Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee, cast El-Sayed's decision to campaign with Harris as both desperate and contradictory, given El-Sayed's past support for the Uncommitted movement.

“Abdul is so desperate that he’s parachuting Kamala Harris into Michigan to save his flailing campaign. Let’s not forget: Abdul led the Uncommitted Movement against Kamala Harris in 2024,” Rogers said in a statement ahead of the visit.

Harris' supporters say her decision to campaign with El-Sayed sends a signal that could help not only him but other prominent Michigan Democrats who were sharply critical of her. Those include Rep. Rashida Tlaib and Alawieh, who is now running for the state legislature.

“She’s being a good Democrat. She has forgiven and is saying ‘it’s time to move on,’” Keith Willians, the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party Black Caucus, told MS NOW. “It can do a lot, because most Black folks didn’t vote for him.”

But some Detroit Democrats doubt that the appearance will move many voters in the country's largest predominantly Black city, especially Black voters who have already tuned out of the race with six weeks to go.

“I find it ironic — folks getting excited about her coming in, but when she was on the ballot, they refused to vote for her,” Detroit City Councilwoman Mary Waters said. “The truth of the matter is she will be preaching to the same choir. Most of the people have checked out of the process.”

Waters knows the city’s electorate well. In addition to serving on the city council, she won the most votes among all council members when seeking re-election, a stat she touts frequently. She generally identifies as a Democrat, but she said she remains undecided in the Senate race and has met with Rogers. El-Sayed plans to meet with her on Wednesday, she said.

To some of Harris' supporters, her return to the campaign trail in Michigan can't be separated from her deliberations over a 2028 presidential run. Michigan was her second-narrowest battleground loss in 2024, after Wisconsin. Another bid would likely require Harris to more clearly define her position on the war in Gaza. But boosting candidates who were once among the fiercest critics of the administration she served in could broaden her appeal.

Waters sees the visit in that light, as outreach aimed more at Arab American voters than Black ones.

“It’s going to massage those relationships in the Arab community for those that didn’t vote for her before, that’s what I think,” she said. “But I don’t know if this will change anything. She still, even if she decides to run for president again, she still will not be able to deliver or commit to their demands, whatever those demands are.”

Sam Baydoun, a Lebanese American member of the Wayne County Commission, told MS NOW that he believes there’s an opening for Harris to run again and win — in Michigan. But not without addressing her 2024 policy positions.

“Especially related to the Middle East and the war in Gaza,” Baydoun said. “I’m not saying that this was the main reason, but it's one of the reasons she lost the election.” He added, “There’s 7 million Biden voters that did not vote in 2024. It wasn’t just the Arab and Muslim community in Michigan, but she needs to form a broad coalition throughout the Democratic base.”

news.title: AOC sure sounds like she’s running for president in 2028: ‘You only get one shot’
news.text:
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez inched closer to a potential 2028 White House run in a new interview that also left open the possibility that she'll challenge powerful fellow New York Democrat Chuck Schumer for his Senate seat.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she told The New York Times. “And you don’t — and just in life in general — life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

But the House's highest-profile progressive said she hasn’t made a decision, which she previously said would come after the crucial November midterm elections for control of Congress.

“Every element of this is something that’s within consideration,” she said.

The remarks, published Tuesday, came during a wide-ranging conversation last week that began when Ocasio-Cortez — widely known as AOC — called a reporter to discuss transferring funds from her $16 million campaign war chest to fellow New York Democrats and campaigning for them upstate, the NYT said.

They also followed comments she made to The Independent in July after a poll showed her with a narrow lead over other potential Democratic contenders in New Hampshire, which holds the nation's first primary elections.

“I think my main focus is really genuinely just the midterms right now, and we have to make sure that we win this majority,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the time.

Neither the Republican National Committee nor a spokesperson for Senate Minority Minority Leader Schumer immediately returned inquiries from The Independent. Schumer, 75, hasn't said if he’ll seek a sixth Senate term.

In August, President Donald Trump told Fox News that he expected AOC to seek the White House after she echoed New York City Council Member Chi Osse's assessment that the pandemic-era “woke 1” movement “was crazy.”

“If you really look at it, they're all saying the same thing,” Trump said, referring to progressive Democrats. “They're all trying to disavow themselves from what they said about crime and, well, they're saying, ‘We love sanctuary cities.’”

At one point in her NYT interview, Ocasio-Cortez — who rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America in August after letting her membership lapse in 2019 — framed the process of deciding whether to run for president in purely subjective terms.

“I think about it personally,” she said. “I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life.”

Ocasio-Cortez, whose mother and paternal grandparents were born in Puerto Rico, also said, “Pretty candidly, I think about my identity.”

“I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina,” she said. “And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.”

Ocasio-Cortez said her gender was "of course" a major factor, noting that women comprise about 27 percent of Congress and no woman has been elected president.

“What is very odd about our political culture is that for some reason when you raise it, people just freak out,” she said. “They get so defensive at the mere suggestion that gender could play a role.”

Trump's defeat of the only two women to secure a presidential nomination — former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in 2016 and then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 — also figures in her thinking, she said.

“It may or may not be related, but I absolutely empathize with the heartbreak that people feel around that and, frankly, how those women were treated,” she said.

Ocasio-Cortez revealed that she'd discussed the issue with Harris, who's also weighing a 2028 White House bid, but declined to discuss their conversations, the NYT said.

AOC won her House seat by ousting an entrenched and powerful incumbent, former Rep. Joe Crowley, and she acknowledged that Democratic control of the Senate could complicate a decision to challenge Schumer.

“That would honestly be the best possible problem we could have as a country,” she said. “We’re working hard to have that problem, and I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.”

Ocasio-Cortez is seeking re-election in November to a fifth term representing her overwhelmingly Democratic district, which covers parts of the Bronx and Queens in New York City.

She's being challenged by Republican Diamant Hysenaj, a real-estate developer and first-time political candidate.

Hysenaj's campaign website plays up his roots on a farm in Kosovo, which his family fled in 1991 when the “communist dictatorship tightened its grip and instability spread across the region.”

Hysenaj had just $31,000 in campaign cash and nearly $28,000 in debts at the end of June, according to the Federal Election Commission.

There aren’t any public polls about the race, but the Cook Political Report rates it solidly in AOC's favor.
news.summary: The progressive New York Democrat has said she’ll decide after the crucial November midterm elections

news.text:

news.title: The Bizarre Backstory of the Trump-Endorsed Sticker Mogul Who Could Be Headed to Congress
news.text:
Anthony Constantino, the Republican nominee in upstate New York’s 21st congressional district, is not subtle in his fealty to Donald Trump. Since 2024, the 43-year-old businessman has given the president a larger-than-life statue of himself, erected a “Vote for Trump” sign massive enough to be seen in satellite images, and dropped an album called “Thank You President Trump” that includes a “Baby Shark”–like track in which he mostly just repeats the president’s name.

Shameless? Yes. Effective? Apparently. This past spring, Trump endorsed the paying Mar-a-Lago member over Assemblyman Robert Smullen, a retired Marine colonel backed by the state party. Constantino—who made a fortune through his novelty company Sticker Mule—defeated Smullen by 19 points. He is now favored to replace the retiring incumbent, Rep. Elise Stefanik.

Such a handoff would be the story of the Trump-era GOP in miniature. Stefanik, who was two grades behind Constantino at Albany Academy, went to Harvard before rocketing up the ranks of the Paul Ryan–era Republican Party. In 2014, she became the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, hailed as a paragon of the party’s supposedly moderate future. After Trump took power, Stefanik tacked hard toward MAGA, only to be rewarded with public humiliation when Trump pulled her nomination to be UN ambassador last year.

Constantino, conversely, says he was “sort of a screwup” as a kid. While Ivy League–educated conservatives have tried to wrangle Trumpism into seminar-table coherence, Constantino—a small-time rapper and boxer—channels MAGA’s gleefully offensive id. During his campaign launch held in front of a wall of free turkeys, Constantino labeled Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez a “perra falsa”—Spanish for fake bitch. He told Gerard Kassar, the head of New York’s Conservative Party, to get “his ass” in a boxing ring, so he could punch him “in the fucking face legally.” In the video for his Zohran Mamdani diss track—e.g., “fuck you bitch,” rapping about the New York mayor’s “boy Osama”—he makes a throat-slitting gesture. In keeping with this thuggish persona, Constantino’s close associates have been accused or found guilty of kidnapping, stealing money from a youth baseball league, and lying to Congress. 

According to Skidmore College political science professor Bob Turner, “when you talk to longtime professional Republicans” in Constantino’s district, they say things “like, ‘I hate that guy. I’m embarrassed by that guy.’” But just as the national establishment did for Trump, the New York GOP is now backing Constantino after failing to stop him. Come January, Constantino could become the most convincing Trump imitator in a body already teeming with them. 

Constantino was born in 1982 to a prominent family in Amsterdam, a small city about a half-hour northwest of Albany. His father was the founder of a successful local printing company, wrote poetry, and was known for advocating on behalf of Native Americans. He died of cancer when Constantino was 6. 

Constantino was a devoted high-school wrestler. Although he lost his first 30 matches, he credits reaching a regional final by reverse-engineering the training of another local wrestler. Today, he is open about imitating Trump. “This is what smart people do,” he says about the president. “We learn from other smart people.”

After high school, he says he was “semi–kicked out” of Stonehill College and transferred to Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, where he left without graduating to work at the family business. In 2010, he co-founded Sticker Mule with a friend of his late father’s. 

The new company brought hundreds of manufacturing jobs to a region where other blue-collar work had disappeared, offering a path to the kind of respect his father enjoyed. But Constantino was not the type to follow one of his dad’s key business precepts: “Don’t promote controversy.” That became clear as the Sticker Mule CEO emerged on Twitter as an outspoken supporter of Trump’s 2016 campaign.

Over the next few years, Constantino began spending most of his time in Mexico training as a boxer. His campaign biography boasts of the “chiseled physique” he developed after taking up the sport professionally, when, at the age of 39, he won a 2022 bout against an opponent who, according to boxing records, never fought professionally before or since. His final—and only third—professional match was a loss the following year to another fighter making his pro debut, a recovering drug addict and candy vendor who has said he was meant to be “carne de cañón” (cannon fodder).

As he pursued boxing, Constantino was also trying to launch what he marketed as a “happy” social media company where users were required to verify their identities before posting. On the site, called Stimulus, his persona was lighthearted, if juvenile; he made at least three posts about eating soups containing animal penis. That was tame compared to a 2024 attempt at stand-up in a Manhattan bar where Constantino described a scenario in which women supporting Kamala Harris vomited before and after he put his penis in their mouths. “I had the consent forms,” Constantino joked.

Within days of winning in 2024, Trump announced his plan to send Stefanik to the UN. Constantino promptly filed to run for her seat, self-funding his anticipated special election campaign with $2.6 million (he has now loaned his campaign $12 million in total). According to FEC filings, some ofthe money went to Drake Ventures, a Florida LLC affiliated with Roger Stone, the former Trump adviser and convicted felon. Other chunks went to PaulAntonelli, a Sticker Mule employee who was arrested for grand larceny in 2020 after being accused of stealing from an Amsterdam youth baseball league. (A police report states $47,000 went missing over a two-year period, much of it from a concession stand. Antonelli pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor.)

When Trump left Stefanik languishing in the House, Constantino retooled for 2026—and grew more aggressive. At a June 2025 campaign event, he insinuated that Kassar may have sent a hit man to murder Antonelli. He alleged that Kassar had told him in late 2025 that “we intend to kill you” and that the Conservative Party would “destroy” him. Constantino added that someone later cut Antonelli’s brake line, suggesting without any clear evidence that Kassar could have been responsible for what he portrayed as a failed murder-for-hire scheme. Kassar later launched an ongoing defamation lawsuit that challenges Constantino’s “wholly false and invented series of events.” Constantino and Antonelli did not respond to requests for comment. 

If Constantino’s allegations sounded like something from GoodFellas, so too did the criminal charges outlined in a police report and court documents against two of his close associates, who were arrested within weeks of his primary victory in connection with the alleged kidnapping and assault of an accountant who also knows the sticker mogul. Matt Moller, the reported victim, says he was one of three friends who attended Constantino’s 2022 wedding. One of the other two, he adds, was Tommy Marcellino—a former MMA fighter who is now accused of abducting and strangling Moller. The second alleged assailant is Ricardo “Porsche Truck Ruk” Henderson, a rapper whom Constantino and affiliated companies have paid more than $500,000 in recent years, according to invoices and emails I reviewed. (Neither of the accused men responded to requests for comment.)

Constantino was not involved in the alleged kidnapping, but it is only the most recent example of people around him being implicated in serious criminal conduct. In late 2025, Constantino used Antonio Brown as a hype man for his Trump album shortly after the former NFL star was extradited from Dubai to face an attempted murder charge in Florida. Jorge Masvidal, another guest star on the record, is a former MMA fighter who pleaded no contest in 2023 to misdemeanor battery after being accused of attacking another UFC fighter outside a Miami restaurant. A third is Jason “Greatness” Jensen, a face-tattooed Sticker Mule brand ambassador who, according to public records, pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2008 before reinventing himself as a Christian rapper.

Constantino’s antics and associations have hurt his standing. In June, the editorial board of the Albany Times Union wrote that it “can’t recall ever meeting a more unsuitable candidate.” An August survey from a local NBC affiliate found that 42 percent of likely voters had a very unfavorable view of Constantino and showed him narrowly trailing Democrat Blake Gendebien, a mild-mannered dairy farmer who lives near the Canadian border. The Sticker Mule CEO again took a page from Trump, saying that it was a “fake poll” and that the FCC should reprimand the station to the “fullest extent possible.” 

A more recent survey touted by Constantino suggested he remains on track to succeed Stefanik. If he does, Constantino has signaled grander ambitions. news.title: No cheery time for election pollsters in run-up to US midterms
news.text:
Pollsters approach this year’s midterm elections dogged by high-profile misfires in recent elections while facing challenges from brash rivals intent on reshaping the landscape of political forecasts.

There are no guarantees that polling’s troubles – and persistent popular skepticism about the dependability of election polls – will be alleviated anytime soon.

In fact, it hasn’t been very cheery for pollsters for the better part of 10 years, since Donald Trump confounded poll-based expectations to defeat Hillary Clinton for the U.S. presidency in 2016. 

In 2020, pollsters turned in their worst collective performance in 40 years by overestimating margins of Joe Biden’s victory over Trump. It’s an outcome I discuss in “Lost in a Gallup,” my book about polling failure.

Polling in the 2022 midterms was more spotty than spectacular. In 2024, pollsters overall underestimated Trump’s popular support — for the third successive election. That outcome prompted The Atlantic to describe the 2024 polls as “quietly still bad.”

Made-up polls

The succession of polling embarrassments was extended in August 2026, in the widely followed Democratic primaries for Senate in Michigan and for governor in Wisconsin. In both races, polls signaled double-digit leads that proved illusory when votes were counted. Those results inspired headlines such as “Should we ever trust polls again?”

August also brought disclosures about fabricated poll results in competitive races in Wisconsin, Nevada and Los Angeles. The bogus polling was the work of a 21-year-old recent college graduate who distributed the invented results through a website called Median Strategies. He said he sought to demonstrate how false survey data can attract wide attention.

Results of one of the sham polls, which claimed Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass was leading by double digits in her reelection bid, were posted on social media by the mayor’s campaign. They also were the subject of newspaper and television reports before being exposed as fraudulent. 

Primary elections are difficult enough for pollsters without the disruption effects of made-up survey results. Primaries typically attract low turnouts, which complicate pollsters’ efforts to estimate who is most likely to vote. 

Betting on elections is not new

Meanwhile, pollsters face pressure from prediction markets such as Kalshi and crypto-based Polymarket, both of which allow participants to wager on election outcomes. 

Betting on U.S. elections has a long if little-recognized pedigree. In 1924, The Wall Street Journal reported from New York that “[s]ome half dozen firms here make a business of receiving and placing bets,” noting that a rule of thumb had emerged that “when odds are more than two to one in a campaign the favored candidate is practically certain to win.”

Wagering on outcomes as a way to forecast election results was supplanted beginning in the 1930s with the emergence of quasi-scientific polling techniques developed by pioneers in survey research such as George Gallup and Elmo Roper. Polls at that time offered what scholars Paul W. Rhode and Koleman S. Strumpf called “a ready substitute for the betting odds, one not subject to the moral objections against gambling.”

In recent years, as polling troubles have deepened, prediction markets have returned from obscurity to become inescapable elements in election forecasting.

Their trading volume, political influence and public profiles have expanded — as have their pretensions. 

Polymarket’s 28-year-old founder, Shayne Coplan, has characterized prediction markets as “the most accurate thing we have as mankind right now.” Coplan also has scoffed at traditional, interview-based surveys, declaring in 2024, “Nobody takes polling seriously anymore.”

Prediction markets can provide real-time probabilities in fluid ways that election polls cannot. But whether such markets pose existential threats to traditional polling is an unsettled question. 

Data journalist Nate Silver has said he doubts whether “prediction markets can serve as a good substitute for polls.” Among the reasons for skepticism is that prediction platform bettors often rely on, and react to, results of preelection polls and poll-based forecasts.

But prediction markets hardly seemed reliant on preelection polls in the 2024 presidential election. Polymarket and Kalshi both predicted Trump’s victory, while polls in aggregate tended to give Vice President Kamala Harris a slight edge.

“Trust the markets, not the polls,” Coplan declared on the social network X soon after the election. Kalshi, meanwhile, proclaimed that its projections favoring Trump “showed how prediction markets can decisively outperform polls and traditional media.” 

Wisconsin’s recent Democratic gubernatorial primary election was, however, something of a comedown for prediction markets. Betting odds on Kalshi and Polymarket gave Francesca Hong a 95% and a 96% chance of winning, respectively. Hong lost, narrowly.

The conundrum of ‘weighting’

Beyond the challenges from prediction markets, pollsters confront the stubborn problem of low response rates. Many people avoid answering pollsters’ overtures, a reality that makes representative samples drawn from surveys alone nearly impossible. This, in turn, obliges pollsters to apply statistical adjustments to their raw data, a process known as “weighting.”

The adjustments are intended to improve accuracy by aligning raw polling data with demographic or political characteristics such as education, race, gender, party registration and how respondents say they voted in the past. But weighting choices vary by pollster and offer no assurance of accuracy.

Josh Clinton, a political scientist at Vanderbilt University, has noted that even “reasonable choices” a pollster may make in weighting can produce marked shifts in a poll’s results. 

Deepening the aggravations in survey research these days is a practice called “silicon sampling,” in which AI agents simulate humanlike poll responses.

Silicon sampling, which has gained prominence in recent months, is much faster and far cheaper to complete than conventional polling. And it has gained a toehold in survey research. 

For instance, Gallup has said it is “exploring the potential of simulated responses” to determine “whether AI systems and emerging methods can help deepen our understanding of how humans think and behave.” 

Silicon sampling troubles some polling traditionalists who are uneasy about ethical and other implications of simulating human responses. 

The 2024 presidential election brought a modest example of silicon sampling in action. AI agents of the startup company Aaru forecast that Harris would carry four of the country’s seven critical swing states. Such an outcome would have given her sufficient electoral votes to be elected president.

Those results, however, were no better than traditional polling in the swing states conducted by CNN and The New York Times. Both organizations reported Harris leading in four states – enough to win had outcomes aligned with their polls.

Harris lost all seven swing states.
news.summary: There are no guarantees that pollsters’ troubles in recent elections and popular skepticism about their dependability will be alleviated anytime soon.

news.title: Kamala Harris seeks to boost progressive Abdul El-Sayed in key Michigan Senate race
news.text:
DETROIT: Former Vice President Kamala Harris will campaign on Tuesday in Michigan in an effort to rally Democratic voters behind progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a swing state that will help determine control of the Senate.

Harris, the first Black person to serve as vice president, is appearing at events in Detroit aimed at building support among Black voters. She will attend a roundtable on Black maternal health with El-Sayed and appear separately at an event hosted by the Detroit chapter of the NAACP, according to her spokesperson.

Her visit comes at a pivotal time in the closely watched Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman. If Democrats hold Michigan’s Senate seat, they’d still need to win four more currently held by the GOP if they are to win control of the 100-member chamber in November. If Rogers wins, their challenge would be even greater.

Rogers has been campaigning in Detroit, a predominantly Black city where his campaign is optimistic he can pick up support from voters hesitant to support El-Sayed. Voters in Wayne County, home to Detroit, supported Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed in the August Democratic primary, favoring the more establishment-aligned Democrat who worked in President Barack Obama’s administration. The stops with Harris, who made history as the nation’s first Black woman to be a major-party presidential nominee, come as El-Sayed is trying to win over voters in the Democratic stronghold.

The race is also seen as a referendum on the viability of a progressive platform on a national level. El-Sayed is running to the left of the Democratic Party establishment, including advocating for universal healthcare and opposing U.S. arms sales to Israel.

Harris’ own relationship with the progressive wing of her party has been strained in the past, particularly as she courted moderate Republican voters during her last presidential campaign, against Republican Donald Trump. Some within her party objected to her support for Israel during the war in Gaza, an issue that has divided Democrats and contributed to Harris’ 2024 loss in Michigan, which has a sizable Arab American population.

El-Sayed is an outspoken critic of Israel who has described the war as a genocide against Palestinians, an accusation rejected by Israel. Some Democratic Jewish voters are supporting Rogers because of El-Sayed’s stance. He has apologized for some past controversial comments and said he is committed to Jewish safety.

Harris’ visit to Michigan also comes as questions swirl about her intentions to run for president in 2028. Harris has not commented on her plans but is also stopping in Nevada and Georgia, two other important states on the political map. Michigan will be the fifth state to vote in the Democratic presidential primary.
news.summary: Kamala Harris will campaign for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to support his bid for the Senate. Her visit includes events to rally Black voter support and discussions on Black maternal health.

news.title: Does Joe Rogan Care Who Wins the Texas Senate Race?
news.text:
It’s late June, more than two hours into the 2,518th episode of his mega-popular podcast, and Joe Rogan is critiquing part of James Talarico’s anatomy.

With his guest, the conservative-leaning comedian Tim Dillon, Rogan was riffing on possible 2028 presidential contenders. Dillon offered up Jon Ossoff, the well-known senior U.S. Senator from Georgia, prompting a “Who’s that guy?” from Rogan. The show’s producer having pulled up a photo of Ossoff, Rogan began to assess.

“That looks like a president. … His neck is medium. It’s not too thin; it’s not too thick,” he said. “Like Talarico’s neck is a little too small, you know what I mean?”

“Yeah, that’s probably true,” replied Dillon.

This bit of neck-related commentary wasn’t turned into viral social media clips or fodder for quick-turn news writeups. But, frequently, Rogan’s off-handed political claims made deep in the woods of his meandering “longform” conversations are indeed treated as newsworthy—part of a long, hard turnaround over the last five years or so.

Gone are the days when presidential contender Bernie Sanders was ostracized for having appeared on the transphobic Rogan’s show and when liberals mounted a campaign for Spotify to deplatform the host over COVID-19 misinformation. Instead, presidential flameout Kamala Harris’ failure to appear on Rogan’s podcast was treated as a major hinge-point in her 2024 collapse. 

And, a little over a year ago, Talarico’s appearance on the show was among the biggest stepping stones in his rise from relatively obscure state rep to hot-shot U.S. Senate nominee. That July 2025 conversation began with Rogan not knowing which elected office Talarico held and ended, 133 minutes later, with the former telling the latter to run for president. “A Joe Rogan-Blessed Democrat? James Talarico Draws Eyes of a Party Desperate For New Leaders,” swiftly blared Time—and even this month GQ described Talarico as “a progressive, Christian state legislator who managed to hang with Joe Rogan.” The out-of-state money and support flowed like Black Rifle coffee during a Rogan podcast.

A month and a half after that episode, Talarico officially declared for Senate. But, over the following year, it’s been unclear whether Rogan supports this bid by the man he told to run for the White House—or even to what extent the Austin-based host is aware of the race that’s unfolding around him. 

Using three separate sites that compile transcripts of Rogan podcast episodes, the Texas Observer identified 20 episodes in which Talarico or his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, were mentioned. A few clear trends emerge. Rogan often brings up Talarico when discussing possible ’28 presidential candidates—and particularly after bashing California Governor Gavin Newsom—rather than anything having to do with the 2026 midterms, in which the Austin state legislator is actually running. And Rogan tends to talk exclusively about Talarico’s position on the Ten Commandments being posted in public schools. As for Paxton, the state’s current attorney general, Rogan largely mentions him as the man who foolishly sued Texas cities for decriminalizing marijuana. 

Despite the largely positive comments on one hand and primarily negative on the other, Rogan usually talks all the way around the fact that the two men are engaged in a high-profile race that one will win and the other lose. Whether through studious avoidance or simple ignorance, he leaves the question open: Does he care who wins the Texas Senate race?

In the episode released on July 18, 2025, Joe Rogan opened by explaining to James Talarico that he’d discovered Talarico when Austin comedian Brian Simpson showed him a video of “some lecture … not a lecture, a speech you were giving about the Ten Commandments in schools.” 

Indeed, Talarico had recently gone viral on social media with a clip from a House floor exchange about Senate Bill 10, which requires public schools to display those principles of Mosaic law.

A few minutes in, perhaps detecting a certain vagueness in Rogan’s introduction and questions, Talarico specified: “I serve here in Austin at the state Capitol,” prompting the question “What is your position?”—to which Talarico responded by explaining the bicameral nature of the state’s legislative branch. 

Talarico, also a Presbyterian seminarian, elaborated his position that forcing Christianity on public school students would turn kids away from religion, and he explained to Rogan the role of big-money Christian nationalists Tim Dunn and Farris Wilks in Texas politics. He also made a biblical case for abortion access, arguing that the Virgin Mary chose to receive Jesus in her womb.

It was then in the middle of a late-episode tangent on government secrecy around Jeffrey Epstein that Rogan somewhat suddenly said, “You need to run for president,” setting in motion the wheels of history. 

Since then, Talarico has come up in at least 10 of Rogan’s podcast shows. There was a September 2025 Matthew McConaughey episode, in which the Texas actor responded skeptically to Rogan’s summation of Talarico’s view on the Ten Commandments issue. “When you look at the commandments, is there anything that anyone out there is going like, ‘I disagree with that one,’” said McConaughey.

Replied Rogan to his producer: “Let’s pull up the Ten Commandments, Jamie”—words that listeners of the show will hear ring in their minds clearer than a bell.

A month later, there was another exchange with National Geographic correspondent Mariana van Zeller, who had heard the Talarico interview and was so enthused that she compared the lawmaker to Martin Luther King Jr., which Rogan seemed to think was a tad much. Then, an episode released that New Year’s Eve with Australian comedian James McCann, in which Rogan called Talarico’s abortion argument “bizarre” and said it “doesn’t jive with how most people view Christianity.” And a February conversation in which another comedian, Matt McCusker, informed Rogan of the then-recent primary spat involving Colin Allred, Talarico, and Jasmine Crockett—producing great confusion on Rogan’s part. 

In general, however, Rogan stuck across these episodes to his script of bringing up Talarico as a favorable contrast to Newsom or to recite the Ten Commandments issue. Among the second category, Rogan engaged Vice President JD Vance in a lengthy July back-and-forth that led to Vance tapping out with a “We can agree to disagree.” 

As for Paxton, the scandal-laden Texas attorney general who defeated incumbent U.S. Senator John Cornyn in a bruising May GOP runoff, the podcast trail extends back a bit further. 

In January 2022, about a year and a half after he moved to Austin from California, Rogan learned who Paxton was from James Lindsay, a Tennessee man who runs the right-wing Twitter account “@ConceptualJames.” (Dialogue: “Who’s that?” “Your attorney general.” “Texas attorney general?” “Yeah.”) Then, two years later, Rogan told comedian Jeff Dye the following about marijuana’s legal status in the Lone Star State: “Apparently it’s decriminalized here in Austin, praise Jesus, but then I heard that Ken Paxton is trying to sue the City of Austin—who I’ve met. He’s a very nice gentleman. Ken, how dare you? … This is stupid, Ken.” 

Across at least eight additional episodes, Rogan generally acknowledged the AG’s existence only to criticize the latter’s stance toward legal weed, other than a passing defense in August 2024 of Paxton’s efforts to root out supposed voter fraud.

Based on this evidentiary record as maintained by Spotify and YouTube, it is possible that Rogan’s political awareness simply begins and ends at the bounds of his own recorded conversations; thus, to him, Talarico and Paxton also start and finish at the edges of his niche interests. It is also possible that—while Rogan explicitly endorsed Donald Trump for president in 2024—he’s intentionally limiting his engagement with this race to avoid blowback from part of his audience. Some of his apparent ignorance, too, could be feigned—a means to stand in for a poorly informed listener. 

It’s hard to guess based on the publicly available material, and his stray comments about politics more broadly do little to clarify.

In both late July and mid-August, Rogan made remarks to the effect that Democrats taking over Texas would be deleterious. “The liberals that want to turn Texas blue, like, don’t. You’re going to ruin it. You’re going to ruin it for you, too. … Balance is important,” he said in the earlier instance. “[Austin is] a liberal city surrounded by like hardcore Republicans with guns and tigers. And it works. … It makes for nice people.” (Talarico responded to this, saying he agrees with the idea and thinks “the best color for Texas is purple.”)

One thing that’s clear: Rogan is haunted by what he sees as the liberal excesses of his former West Coast home state. But what does “balance” look like in a particular race for U.S. Senate, in which the candidates are opposed on issues including, to name one, marijuana legalization? We don’t know, because Rogan won’t let his conversations become specific enough to find out.

Requests for comment sent to an email address and multiple social media accounts associated with Rogan or the podcast went unacknowledged.

This ambiguity came to something of a head in mid-September, when Ron White, the stand-up comic who is sometimes known as Tater Salad and became famous in his days touring with Larry the Cable Guy et al., put the question rather plainly: “So what we gonna do about the Texas Senate—you met Talarico, you liked the guy, right?” 

“I did like him. I liked his thoughts on the Ten Commandments in schools,” answered Rogan, launching into his well-worn spiel.

Then, like a thunderbolt of contextual knowledge, the surprisingly erudite Tater Salad, who hails from a small town in the Texas Panhandle, said that he’d first noticed Talarico when the rep was opposing school vouchers in the Legislature. Apparently unfamiliar, Rogan requested an explanation of the extremely high-profile school privatization scheme, which White provided before concluding: “You really can’t put Ken Paxton back into office in the state of Texas. That guy’s just too corrupt; he’s just a bad egg and we don’t need him around here.” 

Without missing a beat: “There’s a lot of shenanigans with weed in this state right now,” Rogan said, redirecting to his pet Paxton-related topic. 

An hour later, though, White managed to steer the ship back to Talarico, saying the Democrat could be an unusually ethical leader.

“I would hope so,” responded Rogan, before expressing a reservation: “He’s said some things that I think are questionable,” with the subsequent conversation roughly revealing that the “things” are trans participation in competitive sports and gender-affirming treatment for minors. 

White tried to put Rogan’s objection in relative context, summarizing the various scandals that have gotten Paxton sued and impeached over the years. “He’s a criminal, just a piece of shit.”

“I don’t know enough about him,” Rogan replied.

Well, at least there are still a few weeks left to brush up.

news.title: Rabbis ask Kamala Harris to talk to Abdul El-Sayed about their concerns
news.text:
A group of Michigan rabbis and Jewish leaders who earlier urged Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to address concerns among them and their congregants regarding antisemitism and violence are asking former Vice President Kamala Harris to take up their cause with the candidate.

The group, which calls itself Nonnegotiable Michigan, wrote an open letter to Harris dated Sept. 22, as she was set to visit Michigan that day to campaign with El-Sayed.

Earlier in September, the group of rabbis and Jewish leaders had asked El-Sayed, who is Muslim and the son of Egyptian immigrants, to "affirm five baseline commitments to Jewish safety, identity, political participation and self-determination" among Jews in Israel, raising concerns that his criticisms and those of others of Israeli policies have strayed into antisemitic tropes and raised the potential for the threat of violence against the Jewish people.

El-Sayed has repeatedly denounced political or religious violence of any kind and antisemitism specifically. But he has been critical of Israeli policies against the Palestinian people and in its counteroffensive against Hamas in Gaza following the attacks against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. He has repeatedly called for cutting U.S. funding to Israel.

Harris, who ran unsuccessfully as the Democratic nominee for president in 2024, remained supportive of U.S. aid to Israel, though she committed to try to end the fighting in Gaza. El-Sayed, despite his criticism of Israel, endorsed Harris after she stepped in to run in place of then-President Joe Biden.

In the letter, the group noted that Harris "never asked us to choose between our commitment to social justice and our Jewish safety or identity" and that she and her husband, who is Jewish, "led the efforts to produce the first-ever national strategy to combat antisemitism." They said their pleas to El-Sayed, on the other hand, have "been met with silence."

"We believe he needs to be urged by Democratic Party leaders who understand that Jews have been one of the strongest, most committed voting blocs in the Democratic coalition; and by someone who understands that a Democratic Party that is not safe for Jews will not be able to protect our democracy," the letter said.

The Jewish community in Michigan has been split, however, on El-Sayed's candidacy and his criticism of Israeli policies toward Palestinians.

While some Jewish Democrats have talked openly about voting for Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in the Nov. 3 election, others have defended El-Sayed, including progressive Jewish voters, at least one of whom called the earlier Nonnegotiable Michigan letter an "insult," as more mainstream Democrats have coalesced around El-Sayed's candidacy. Another 600 Michigan Jewish voters signed a letter pledging to support El-Sayed.

El-Sayed's campaign announced that Harris was expected to join him on Tuesday, Sept. 22, for a roundtable discussion about maternal health issues for Black women. No other details had been immediately provided about the time and place of the event.

news.title: Deprogrammed: Believe the Democrats Who Got Out
news.text:
Maya Angelou's old rule still holds: when someone shows you who they are, believe them the first time. Two former Democratic insiders showed us exactly who runs their party's machinery this week, and most of the press answered with a shrug.

Jake Altman, a former executive board member of the Democratic Socialists of America's (DSA) Boston chapter, told Fox News he walked because the group started sounding like the "extreme groups on the Left" he'd joined DSA to avoid. The same week, former Democratic National Committee fundraiser Lindy Li told Fox News that Kamala Harris ran a "charade" on major donors days before Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 race, assuring them Biden would stay in while quietly courting the same donors for herself. Different corners of the party, same story: a leadership class that manages the narrative and freezes out anyone who won't play along.

I've spent 15 years as a designated expert witness in fiduciary duty litigation, testifying in federal and state courts about what happens when insiders conceal material facts from the people who trust them. The pattern never changes. Somebody in charge knows something the principal doesn't and manages the information flow to protect their own position. What Altman and Li describe is a breach of the duty of candor, applied to a party instead of a trust account, with voters as the shortchanged beneficiaries.

Altman's account carries the kind of checkable detail that separates testimony from talking points. He points to the 2017 resignation of DSA committee member Danny Fetonte after members learned of his past work for a Texas police union, and a 2019 internal fight in which he pushed DSA to denounce Nicolás Maduro and watched the group defend him instead. His verdict: "dissident voices have been silenced," and most of the dissidents left. That's an organization running on loyalty tests, the same mechanism I've watched sink family businesses and investment partnerships when a founder can't absorb a correction.

Li's account runs the identical play at a higher altitude. She says Harris told donors point blank there was no daylight between her and Biden, then launched a "charm offensive" on that same donor list the moment he stepped aside. Li calls the environment a cult, one where asking where the money went got you frozen out. I've watched fund managers handle skeptical limited partners the same way. The tactic isn't new. It's just rarely aimed at an entire presidential campaign.

Skeptics will note that Altman has one grievance and Li has a book to sell, so the incentive deserves scrutiny alongside the testimony. Fair, and I'd say the same to a jury. But testimony strengthens when independent witnesses with no relationship to each other describe the same conduct from different vantage points. Joe Manchin left the party in 2024 over partisanship that crowded out the middle. Kyrsten Sinema did the same in 2022, citing party-line pressure over independent judgment. Andrew Yang quit in 2021 and started the Forward Party over a two-party incentive structure he'd concluded was broken. Tulsi Gabbard left the same year, calling the party an "elitist cabal" answering to ideologues instead of voters. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Elon Musk, a career Democratic donor, both walked for reasons ranging from health orthodoxy to censorship, and both describe the identical mechanism: raise the wrong question, get managed out.

Here's where the press's selective appetite for transformation stories shows itself. A personal transition earns a sympathetic profile in every outlet with a pulse. A hardened DSA board member or a top-tier fundraiser describing a machine that freezes out dissent gets newsroom silence dressed up as balance. That's not journalism. That's choosing which whistles get blown.

None of this makes every defector right about everything. Li's claim about a rigged internal poll ranking Harris last among potential replacements remains an allegation, not a document, and a fair reader holds it at that level until one surfaces. But the pattern across Altman, Li, Manchin, Sinema, Yang, and Gabbard isn't coincidence or partisan spin. It's a consistent account, from people who had every incentive to stay quiet and cash in on loyalty instead, describing an institution built to manage appearances rather than earn trust.

Angelou's rule cuts both ways. When a party's own former insiders keep showing you the same mechanism, from the ward level to the West Wing, the honest response is to stop assuming exaggeration and start asking why so many are saying it at once. That's not a hunch. It's a pattern of material nondisclosure, and the remedy starts the moment the people who used to guard the secrets decide they're done guarding them.
